data.content:
Finance term: Effects of Unanticipated and Anticipated Policy,New Classical Macroeconomic Model
Definition: The response to an unanticipated increase in the money supply can be analyzed through the short-run aggregate supply curve AS_{1}, drawn for an expected price level P_{1}. Initially, the aggregate demand curve AD_{1} intersects AS_{1} at point 1, resulting in an expected price level P_{1} and aggregate output at the natural rate level Y_{n}. At this point, which is also on the long-run aggregate supply curve, the economy is in long-run equilibrium, with no tendency for shifts in aggregate supply.

Should the Fed unexpectedly increase the money supply through a large open market purchase, the aggregate demand curve shifts rightward to AD_{2}. Since this shift is unexpected, the expected price level remains at P_{1}, and the short-run aggregate supply curve continues to be AS_{1}. The new equilibrium occurs at point 2’ where the intersection of AD_{2} and AS_{1} yields aggregate output at Y_{2’} and a realized price level of P_{2’}, indicating an increase in output above the natural rate.

Conversely, if the public anticipates the Fed's action based on historical behavior, expectations shift. Workers and firms, recognizing the impending expansionary policy, expect the aggregate price level to rise to P_{2}. In response, workers will demand higher wages to maintain their real earnings as prices increase. This leads to a leftward shift of the short-run aggregate supply curve to AS_{2}, resulting in the new equilibrium at point 2, where AD_{2} intersects AS_{2}. In this scenario, aggregate output returns to the natural rate level Y_{n}, though the price level rises to P_{2}.

The new classical macroeconomic model illustrates that anticipated expansionary policy does not lead to an increase in aggregate output; rather, it moves the economy to a long-run equilibrium (point 2) at the natural rate level. The model's classical aspect arises from the fact that anticipated policies do not alter aggregate output. Aggregate output can only deviate from the natural rate as a result of unanticipated changes in the aggregate demand curve.

The policy ineffectiveness proposition summarizes a key conclusion: anticipated policy has no effect on the business cycle, with only unanticipated policy affecting output. Although anticipated policy does not result in output fluctuations, unanticipated changes—in contrast—will have significant effects on aggregate output.

Finance term: relationship between default risk and risk premium,Default Risk,Risk Structure of Interest Rates
Definition: Our supply and demand analysis of the bond market can be used to explain why a bond with default risk always has a positive risk premium and why the higher the default risk is, the larger the risk premium will be.
To examine the effect of default risk on interest rates, let us look at the supply and demand diagrams for the default-free (U.S. Treasury) and corporate long-term bond markets in Figure 2. To make the diagrams somewhat easier to read, let's assume that initially corporate bonds have the same default risk as U.S. Treasury bonds. In this case, these two bonds have the same attributes (identical risk and maturity); their equilibrium prices and interest rates will initially be equal (P_{1}^{c}=P_{1}^{T} and i_{1}^{c}=i_{1}^{T}), and the risk premium on corporate bonds (i_{1}^{c}-i_{1}^{T}) will be zero.
If the possibility of a default increases because a corporation begins to suffer large losses, the default risk on corporate bonds will increase, and the expected return on these bonds will decrease. In addition, the corporate bonds return will be more uncertain. The theory of asset demand predicts that because the expected return on the corporate bond falls relative to the expected return on the default-free Treasury bond while its relative riskiness rises, the corporate bond is less desirable (holding everything else equal), and demand for it will fall. Another way of thinking about this is that if you were an investor, you would want to hold (demand) a smaller amount of corporate bonds. The demand curve for corporate bonds in panel (a) of Figure 2 then shifts to the left, from to D_{1}^{c} to D_{2}^{c}.
At the same time, the expected return on default-free Treasury bonds increases relative to the expected return on corporate bonds, while their relative riskiness declines. The Treasury bonds thus become more desirable, and demand rises, as shown in panel (b) by the rightward shift in the demand curve for these bonds from D_{1}^{T} to D_{2}^{T}.
As we can see in Figure 2, the equilibrium price for corporate bonds falls from P_{1}^{c} to P_{2}^{c}, and since the bond price is negatively related to the interest rate, the equilibrium interest rate on corporate bonds rises to i_{2}^{c}. At the same time, however, the equilibrium price for the Treasury bonds rises from P_{1}^{T} to P_{2}^{T} and the equilibrium interest rate falls to i_{2}^{T}. The spread between the interest rates on corporate and default-free bonds--that is, the risk premium on corporate bonds--has risen from zero to i_{2}^{c}-i_{2}^{T}.

data.content:
Finance term: cash flow mapping and,Value at risk (VaR)
Definition: It is out of the question in the model-building approach to define a separate market variable for every single bond price or interest rate to which a company is exposed. Some simplifications are necessary when the model-building approach is used. One possibility is to assume that only parallel shifts in the yield curve occur. It is then necessary to define only one market variable: the size of the parallel shift. The changes in the value of a bond portfolio can then be calculated using the duration relationship

\[\Delta P=-DP\Delta y\]

where \(P\) is the value of the portfolio, \(\Delta P\) is the change in \(P\) in one day, \(D\) is the modified duration of the portfolio, and \(\Delta y\) is the parallel shift in 1 day.

This approach does not usually give enough accuracy. The procedure usually followed is to choose as market variables the prices of zero-coupon bonds with standard maturities: 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, 5 years, 7 years, 10 years, and 30 years. For the purposes of calculating VaR, the cash flows from instruments in the portfolio are mapped into cash flows occurring on the standard maturity dates. Consider a $1 million position in a Treasury bond lasting 1.2 years that pays a coupon of 6% semiannually. Coupons are paid in 0.2, 0.7, and 1.2 years, and the principal is paid in 1.2 years. This bond is, therefore, in the first instance regarded as a $30,000 position in 0.2-year zero-coupon bond plus a $30,000 position in a 0.7-year zero-coupon bond plus a $1.03 million position in a 1.2-year zero-coupon bond.

 The position in the 0.2-year bond is then replaced by an approximately equivalent position in 1-month and 3-month zero-coupon bonds; the position in the 0.7-year bond is replaced by an approximately equivalent position in 6-month and 1-year zero-coupon bonds; and the position in the 1.2-year bond is replaced by an approximately equivalent position in 1-year and 2-year zero-coupon bonds. The result is that the position in the 1.2-year coupon-bearing bond is for VaR purposes regarded as a position in zero-coupon bonds having maturities of 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years.

This procedure is known as _cash-flow mapping_. One way of doing it is explained in Technical Note 25 at www.rotman.utoronto.ca/\(\sim\)hull/TechnicalNotes. Note that cash-flow mapping is not necessary when the historical simulation approach is used. This is because the complete term structure of interest rates can be calculated from the variables that are considered for each of the scenarios generated.

data.content:
Finance term: valuing,Forward contract
Definition: The article lays out theoretical assumptions and mathematical formulations related to forward and futures contracts. Specific assumptions for market participants include the absence of transaction costs, uniform tax rates on net trading profits, equal borrowing and lending rates at the risk-free rate, and the active pursuit of arbitrage opportunities.

Key notations are introduced:
- \( T \): Time until the delivery date of a contract (in years)
- \( S_{0} \): Current price of the underlying asset
- \( F_{0} \): Forward price today
- \( r \): Zero-coupon risk-free interest rate per annum with continuous compounding

The delivery price \( K \) is set when the contract is negotiated, remaining fixed over time, while the current forward price \( F_{0} \) varies, affecting the contract's value \( f \). The general result for the value of a long forward contract is given by:

\[
f = (F_{0} - K)e^{-rT} \tag{5.4}
\]

This equation is derived by forming a risk-free portfolio consisting of two forward contracts, leading to a certain total payoff of \( F_{0} - K \) at time \( T \). The present value of this payoff, discounted at the risk-free rate, is \( (F_{0} - K)e^{-rT} \). The value of a long forward contract is thus the present value of the expected payoff, while a short forward contract's value is:

\[
(K - F_{0})e^{-rT}
\]

For an investment asset that provides no income, the value of a forward contract can be expressed as:

\[
f = S_{0} - Ke^{-rT} \tag{5.5}
\]

When the asset generates known income with present value \( I \):

\[
f = S_{0} - I - Ke^{-rT} \tag{5.6}
\]

For an asset providing a known yield at rate \( q \):

\[
f = S_{0}e^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT} \tag{5.7}
\]

Additionally, the effects of changes in futures prices on gains or losses are highlighted, where the gain or loss from a futures contract is computed as the change in futures price multiplied by the size of the position. The relationship established in equation (5.4) shows that for forward contracts, the gain or loss is the present value of the change in forward price times the size of the position, emphasizing the timing of realizations in futures trading due to daily settlements. 

Overall, the equations presented provide a comprehensive analytical framework for understanding how forward and futures contracts are valued based on price movements of the underlying asset and prevailing interest rates.

data.content:
Finance term: rational expectations,The Theory of Rational Expectations
Definition: **Rational expectations** can be stated as follows: **Expectations will be identical to optimal forecasts** (_the best guess of the future_) **using all available information.
Formally, if X stands for the variable that is being forecast, X^{e} for the expectation of this variable, and X^{of} for the optimal forecast of X using all available information (the best guess possible of his driving time), the theory of rational expectations then simply says
X^{e}=X^{of}
That is, the expectation of X equals the optimal forecast using all available information.
Rational Behind the Theory: The incentives for equating expectations with optimal forecasts are especially strong in financial markets. In these markets, people with better forecasts of the future get rich. The application of the theory of rational expectations to financial markets (where it is called the **efficient market hypothesis** or the **theory of efficient capital markets**) is thus particularly useful.
Implications of the Theory are as follows:
1. _If there is a change in the way a variable moves, the way in which expectations of this variable are formed will change as well_.
2. _The forecast errors of expectations will, on average, be zero and cannot be predicted ahead of time_.

question: Consider the relationship between bond price, coupon rate, YTM, and current yield.For discount bonds, the YTM exceeds the coupon rate.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: values,Bonds
Definition: Just like any financial instrument, bonds are affected by fluctuations in interest rates. As marketplace interest rates change, the cash flows from a bond remain constant, leading to variations in the bond's market value. When interest rates rise, the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows declines, reducing its value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, the bond's value increases.

To accurately assess the value of a bond at any given time, it is crucial to know the following: the number of periods remaining until maturity, the bond's face value, the coupon payments, and the prevailing market interest rate for similar bonds. This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

Just like any financial instrument, bonds are affected by fluctuations in interest rates. As marketplace interest rates change, the cash flows from a bond remain constant, leading to variations in the bond's market value. When interest rates rise, the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows declines, reducing its value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, the bond's value increases.

To accurately assess the value of a bond at any given time, it is crucial to know the following: the number of periods remaining until maturity, the bond's face value, the coupon payments, and the prevailing market interest rate for similar bonds. This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

data.content:
Finance term: one-step,Binomial tree
Definition: A no-arbitrage framework for pricing options on a stock is presented, where the stock price is denoted as \(S_{0}\) and the current option price as \(f\). The option has a lifespan of time \(T\), during which the stock price can move to either \(S_{0}u\) (up movement, with \(u>1\)) or \(S_{0}d\) (down movement, with \(d<1\)). The percentage changes in the stock price are represented by \(u-1\) for upward movement and \(1-d\) for downward movement. The payoffs from the option under upward and downward movements are \(f_{u}\) and \(f_{d}\) respectively.

To eliminate risk from a portfolio consisting of \(\Delta\) shares and a short position in one option, the value expressions for the portfolio can be calculated. For an up movement, the portfolio value becomes:

\[
S_{0}u\Delta - f_{u}
\]

For a down movement, it becomes:

\[
S_{0}d\Delta - f_{d}
\]

Setting these values equal to each other results in:

\[
S_{0}u\Delta - f_{u} = S_{0}d\Delta - f_{d}
\]

From which we can derive:

\[
\Delta = \frac{f_{u} - f_{d}}{S_{0}u - S_{0}d} \tag{13.1}
\]

In a no-arbitrage context, the portfolio should earn the risk-free interest rate, denoted as \(r\). The present value of the portfolio is given by:

\[
(S_{0}u\Delta - f_{u})e^{-rT}
\]

The cost of establishing the portfolio is:

\[
S_{0}\Delta - f
\]

Equating the cost with the present value leads to:

\[
S_{0}\Delta - f = (S_{0}u\Delta - f_{u})e^{-rT}
\]

Rearranging provides:

\[
f = S_{0}\Delta(1 - ue^{-rT}) + f_{u}e^{-rT}
\]

Substituting \(\Delta\) from equation (13.1) results in:

\[
f = S_{0}\bigg{(}\frac{f_{u} - f_{d}}{S_{0}u - S_{0}d}\bigg{)}(1 - ue^{-rT}) + f_{u}e^{-rT}
\]

This can be simplified to:

\[
f = \frac{f_{u}(1 - de^{-rT}) + f_{d}(ue^{-rT} - 1)}{u - d} \tag{13.2}
\]

We also introduce \(p\) defined as:

\[
p = \frac{e^{rT} - d}{u - d} \tag{13.3}
\]

The derived equations (13.2) and (13.3) provide a method for pricing an option based on stock price movements as described by a one-step binomial tree, with the critical assumption of no arbitrage opportunities in the market.

Definition: Once a loan has been made, the borrower has an incentive to engage in risky activities that make it less likely that the loan will be paid off. To reduce this moral hazard, financial institutions must adhere to the principle for managing credit risk that a lender should write provisions (restrictive covenants) into loan contracts that restrict borrowers from engaging in risky activities. By monitoring borrowers' activities to see whether they are complying with the restrictive covenants and by enforcing the covenants if they are not, lenders can make sure that borrowers are not taking on risks at their expense. The need for banks and other financial institutions to engage in screening and monitoring explains why they spend so much money on auditing and information-collecting activities.

question: A distribution with a heavier left tail and less heavy right tail than the lognormal distribution gives rise to a downward sloping volatility smile.The less heavy right tail should lead to low prices, and therefore low volatilities for out-of-the-money (high-strike-price) calls.

data.content:
Finance term: equity option,Black–Scholes–Merton and volatility smile
Definition: Prior to the crash of 1987, there was no marked volatility smile for equity options. Since 1987, the volatility smile used by traders to price equity options (both on individual stocks and on stock indices) has had the general form shown in Figure 20.3. This is sometimes referred to as a _volatility skew_. The volatility decreases as the strike price increases. The volatility used to price a low-strike-price option (i.e., a deep-out-of-the-money put or a deep-in-the-money call) is significantly higher than that used to price a high-strike-price option (i.e., a deep-in-the-money put or a deep-out-of-the-money call).

The volatility smile for equity options corresponds to the implied probability distribution given by the solid line in Figure 20.4. A lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as the implied distribution is shown by the dotted line. It can be seen that the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a less heavy right tail than the lognormal distribution.

To see that Figures 20.3 and 20.4 are consistent with each other, we proceed as for Figures 20.1 and 20.2 and consider options that are deep out of the money. From Figure 20.4, a deep-out-of-the-money call with a strike price of \(K_{2}\) has a lower price when the implied distribution is used than when the lognormal distribution is used. This is because the option pays off only if the stock price proves to be above \(K_{2}\), and the probability of this is lower for the implied probability distribution than for the lognormal distribution. Therefore, we expect the implied distribution to give a relatively low price for the option. A relatively low price leads to a relatively low implied volatility--and this is exactly what we observe in Figure 20.3 for the option. Consider next a deep-out-of-the-money put option with a strike price of \(K_{1}\). This option pays off only if the stock price proves to be below \(K_{1}\). Figure 20.4 shows that the probability of this is higher for the implied probability distribution than for the lognormal distribution. We therefore expect the implied distribution to give a relatively high price, and a relatively high implied volatility, for this option. Again, this is exactly what we observe in Figure 20.3.

### The Reason for the Smile in Equity Options

One possible explanation for the smile in equity options concerns leverage. As a company's equity declines in value, the company's leverage increases. This means that the equity becomes more risky and its volatility increases. As a company's equity increases in value, leverage decreases. The equity then becomes less risky and its volatility decreases. This argument suggests that we can expect the volatility of a stock to be a decreasing function of the stock price and is consistent with Figures 20.3 and 20.4. Another explanation is "crashophobia\”.

data.content:
Finance term: Cox–Ingersoll–Ross,Interest rate models
Definition: Cox, Ingersoll, and Ross (CIR) have proposed the following alternative model:5

Footnote 5: See J. C. Cox, J. E. Ingersoll, and S. A. Ross, “A Theory of the Term Structure of Interest Rates,” _Econometrica_, 53 (1985): 385–407.

\[dr=a(b-r)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt{r}\,dz\]

where \(a\), \(b\), and \(\sigma\) are nonnegative constants. This has the same mean-reverting drift as Vasicek, but the standard deviation of the change in the short rate in a short period of time is proportional to \(\sqrt{r}\). This means that, as the short-term interest rate increases, the standard deviation increases.

Bond prices in the CIR model have the same general form as those in Vasicek's model,

\[P(t,T)=A(t,T)e^{-B(t,T)r(t)}\]

but the functions \(B(t,T)\) and \(A(t,T)\) are different:

\[B(t,T)=\frac{2(e^{\gamma(T-t)}-1)}{(\gamma+a)(e^{\gamma(T-t)}-1)+2\gamma}\]

and

\[A(t,T)=\left[\frac{2\gamma e^{(a+\gamma)(T-t)/2}}{(\gamma+a)(e^{\gamma(T-t)}-1 )+2\gamma}\right]^{2ab/\sigma^{2}}\]

with \(\gamma=\sqrt{a^{2}+2\sigma^{2}}\).

To see this result, we substitute \(m=a(b-r)\) and \(s=\sigma\sqrt{r}\) into differential equation (31.5) to get

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+a(b-r)\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}+\tfrac{1}{2} \sigma^{2}r\frac{\partial f}{\partial r^{2}}=rf\]

As in the case of Vasicek's model, we can prove the bond-pricing result by substituting \(f=A(t,T)e^{-B(t,T)r}\) into the differential equation. In this case, \(A(t,T)\) and \(B(t,T)\) are solutions of

\[B_{t}-aB-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}B^{2}+1=0,\quad A_{t}-abAB=0\]

Furthermore, the boundary condition \(P(T,T)=1\) is satisfied.

Definition: The bank itself might default. This is liable to lead to a loss to the counterparty together with an equal and opposite gain to the bank. The debit (or debt) value adjustment (DVA) is the present value of the expected gain to the bank from its own default. It is calculated similarly to CVA: \\[\\text{DVA}=\\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_{i}^{*}v_{i}^{*}\\] where \\(q_{i}^{*}\\) is the probability of a default by the bank during the \\(i\\)th interval and \\(v_{i}^{*}\\) is the present value of the bank's gain (and the counterparty's loss) if the bank defaults at the midpoint of the interval. Taking both CVA and DVA into account, the value of the portfolio to the bank is \\[f_{\\text{nd}}-\\text{CVA}+\\text{DVA}\\]

Finance term: agency problem and,Financial management goals
Definition: To see how management and stockholder interests might differ, imagine that the firm is considering a new investment. The new investment is expected to favorably impact the share value, but it is also a relatively risky venture. The owners of the firm will wish to take the investment (because the stock value will rise), but management may not because there is the possibility that things will turn out badly and management jobs will be lost. If management does not take the investment, then the stockholders may lose a valuable opportunity. This is one example of an agency cost. \n\n It is sometimes argued that, left to themselves, managers would tend to maximize the amount of resources over which they have control or, more generally, corporate power or wealth. This goal could lead to an overemphasis on corporate size or growth. For example, cases in which management is accused of overpaying to buy up another company just to increase the size of the business or to demonstrate corporate power are not uncommon. Obviously, if overpayment does take place, such a purchase does not benefit the stockholders of the purchasing company.

A portfolio beta, however, can be calculated, just like a portfolio expected return. For example, looking again at Table 13.8, suppose you put half of your money in Exxon-Mobil and half in Yahoo!. What would the beta of this combination be? Because ExxonMobil has a beta of .85 and Yahoo! has a beta of 1.80, the portfolio's beta, b_pr_, would be:

Finance term: portfolio insurance,Index futures
Definition: A portfolio manager often seeks to acquire put options for portfolio protection against market declines while maintaining potential gains in positive market conditions. One method is purchasing put options on market indices like the S&P 500. Alternatively, options can be created synthetically through a position in the underlying asset or futures, allowing the delta of the position to match the delta of the desired option. The creation of a synthetic option is the reverse of the hedging process.

Creating synthetic options may be more appealing for portfolio managers due to two factors: limited liquidity in option markets for large fund transactions and the unavailability of necessary strike prices and exercise dates in exchange-traded options. 

To synthesize a put option by trading the portfolio, the delta of a European put is given by:

\[
\Delta = e^{-qT}[N(d_{1})-1]
\]

where 

\[
d_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K)+(r-q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},
\]

with \(S_{0}\) as the portfolio value, \(K\) as the strike price, \(r\) as the risk-free rate, \(q\) as the dividend yield, \(\sigma\) as the portfolio volatility, and \(T\) as the option's lifespan. Portfolio volatility can generally be estimated as its beta multiplied by the volatility of a well-diversified market index.

To create a put option synthetically, the fund manager needs to sell a proportion:

\[
e^{-qT}[1-N(d_{1})]
\]

of the original portfolio's stocks and invest the proceeds in riskless assets. As the original portfolio’s value declines, the delta of the put becomes more negative, requiring an increase in sold portfolio proportions. Conversely, as the portfolio value increases, the delta becomes less negative, necessitating a reduction in sold proportions, i.e., repurchasing part of the original portfolio.

Using this strategy divides funds between the stock portfolio needing insurance and riskless assets. When the stock portfolio value rises, riskless assets are sold to increase stock positions. When it declines, the position in stocks is reduced, and riskless assets are bought. The cost of this insurance comes from consistently selling after declines and purchasing after increases in market value.

Utilizing index futures to create synthetic options can be advantageous due to generally lower transaction costs compared to trading in underlying stocks. The dollar amount of futures contracts shorted relative to the portfolio value is determined by:

\[
e^{-qT}e^{-(r-q)T^{*}}[1-N(d_{1})]=e^{q(T^{*}-T)}e^{-rT^{*}}[1-N(d_{1})]
\]

where \(T^{*}\) signifies the futures contract's maturity. If the portfolio is valued at \(A_{1}\) times the index, and each futures contract is on \(A_{2}\) times the index, the required number of shorted futures contracts is computed as:

\[
e^{q(T^{*}-T)}e^{-rT^{*}}[1-N(d_{1})]A_{1}/A_{2}.
\]

This analysis presumes the portfolio mirrors the index. If not, a calculation of the portfolio's beta is necessary, alongside determining the position in options on the index for necessary protection and the chosen position in index futures to create the options synthetically. The strike price for the options should reflect the expected market index level when the portfolio reaches its insured value, with the number of options being beta times the amount needed for a portfolio with a beta of 1.0.

data.content:
Finance term: efficient market hypothesis,The Efficient Market Hypothesis: Rational Expectations in Financial Markets
Definition: The efficient market hypothesis is based on the assumption that prices of securities in financial markets fully reflect all available information. Recall that the rate of return from holding a security equals the sum of the capital gain on the security (the change in the price), plus any cash payments, divided by the initial purchase price of the security:
R = \frac{P_{t + 1} - P_{t} + C}{P_{t}}
where 
R = rate of return on the security held from time t to t+1 (say, the end of 2010 to the end of 2011)
P_{t+1} = price of the security at time t+1, the end of the holding period 
P_{t} = price of the security at time t, the beginning of the holding period 
C = cash payment (coupon or dividend payments) made in the period t to t+1
Let's look at the expectation of this return at time t, the beginning of the holding period. Because the current price P_{t} and the cash payment C are known at the beginning, the only variable in the definition of the return that is uncertain is the price next period, P_{t+1}. Denoting the expectation of the security's price at the end of the holding period as P_{t+1}^{e}, the expected return R^{e} is
R^{e} = P_{t+1}^{e} - P_{t} + C
The efficient market hypothesis views expectations of future prices as equal to optimal forecasts using all currently available information. In other words, the markets expectations of future securities prices are rational, so that
P_{t+1}^{e} = P_{t+1}^{of}
which in turn implies that the expected return on the security will equal the optimal forecast of the return:
R^{e} = R^{of}
Unfortunately, we cannot observe either R^{e} or P_{t+1}^{e}, so the rational expectations equations by themselves do not tell us much about how the financial market behaves. However, supply and demand analysis enables us to determine the expected return on a security using the equilibrium return R^*; this is, R^e=R^*. Replacing R^e with R^*, we get R^{of}=R^*.
Rational Behind the Hypothesis is as follows:
Denote the optimal forecast of the return and the equilibrium return as R^{of} and R^*, respectively. The rational behind the efficient market hypothesis are summarized as follows:
R_{of} > R^* --> increase in the current stock price P_t --> decrease in R_{of}
R_{of} < R^* --> decrease in the current stock price P_t --> increase in R_{of}
until R^{of}=R^*.

question: Consider the importance of policy expectations to movements of the aggregate supply curve.If expectations about policy do not matter, pursuing a nonaccommodating, nonactivist policy does not have the hidden benefit of making it less likely that workers will push up their wages and create unemployment.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Do Expectations Favor Nondiscretionary Policy?,Expectations and the Discretionary/Nondiscretionary Debate
Definition: Does the possibility that expectations about policy matter to the wage-setting process strengthen the case for nondiscretionary policy? The case for discretionary policy states that with slow wage and price adjustment, the discretionary policy returns the economy to full employment at point 2 far more quickly than it takes to get to full employment at point 1 if nothing is done. However, the argument for discretionary policy does not allow for the possibility (1) that expectations about policy matter to the wage-setting process and (2) that the economy might initially have moved from point 1 to point 1' because an attempt by workers to raise their wages or a negative supply shock shifted the short-run aggregate supply curve from \\(AS_{2}\\) to \\(AS_{1}\\). We must therefore ask the following question about discretionary policy: Will the short-run aggregate supply curve continue to shift to the left after the economy has reached point 2, leading to cost-push inflation?
The answer to this question is yes if expectations about policy matter. Our discussion of cost-push inflation in Figure 5 suggested that if workers know that policy will be accommodating in the future, they will continue to push their wages up, and the short-run aggregate supply curve will keep shifting leftward. As a result, policymakers are forced to accommodate the cost push by continuing to shift the aggregate demand curve to the right to eliminate the unemployment that develops. The accommodating, discretionary policy with its high employment target has the hidden cost or disadvantage that it may well lead to inflation.
The main advantage of a nonaccommodating, nondiscretionary policy, in which policymakers do not try to shift the aggregate demand curve in response to the cost push, is that it will prevent inflation. As depicted in Figure 4, the result of an upward push on wages in the face of a nonaccommodating, nondiscretionary policy will be a period of unemployment above the natural rate level, which will eventually shift the short-run aggregate supply curve and the price level back to their initial positions. The main criticism of this policy is that the economy will suffer protracted periods of unemployment when the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts leftward. Workers, however, would probably not push for higher wages to begin with if they knew that policy would be nonaccommodating, because their wage gains will lead to a protracted period of unemployment. A nonaccommodating, nondiscretionary policy may have not only the advantage of preventing inflation but also the hidden benefit of discouraging leftward shifts in the short-run aggregate supply curve that lead to excessive unemployment.
In conclusion, **if workers' opinions about whether policy is accommodating or nonaccommodating matter to the wage-setting process, the case for discretionary policy is much weaker**.

data.content:
Finance term: Zions Bancorp,Employee stock option
Definition: One way of valuing an employee stock option is to see what the market would pay for it. Cisco was the first to try this in 2006. It proposed selling options with the exact terms of its employee stock options to institutional investors. This approach was rejected by the SEC on the grounds that the range of investors bidding for the options was not wide enough.

Zions Bancorp has suggested an alternative approach. It proposed that securities providing payoffs mirroring those actually realized by its employees be sold. Suppose that the strike price for a particular grant to employees is $40 and it turns out that 1% of employees exercise after exactly 5 years when the stock price is $60, 2% exercise after exactly 6 years when the stock price is $65, and so on. Then 1% of the securities owned by an investor will provide a $20 payoff after 5 years, 2% will provide a payoff of $25 after 6 years, and so on.

Zions Bancorp tested the idea using its own stock option grant to its employees. It sold the securities using a Dutch auction process. In this individuals or companies can submit a bid indicating the price they are prepared to pay and the number of options they are prepared to buy. The clearing price is the highest bid such that the aggregate number of options sought at that price or a higher price equals or exceeds the number of options for sale. Buyers who have bid more than the clearing price get their orders filled at the clearing price and the buyer who bid the clearing price gets the remainder. Zions Bancorp announced that it had received SEC approval for its market-based approach in October 2007, but the approach has not been used to any great extent.

question: Consider the valuation methods of different types of interest rate swaps.For a compounding swap, there is no approximation used when the "assume forward rates are realized" rule is applied.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Compounding swap
Definition: In a compounding swap, interest on one or both sides is compounded forward to the end of the life of the swap according to preagreed rules and there is only one payment date at the end of the life of the swap.

 Another variation on the plain vanilla swap is a _compounding swap_. A hypothetical confirmation for a compounding swap is in Business Snapshot 33.2. In this example there is only one payment date for both the floating-rate payments and the fixed-rate payments. This is at the end of the life of the swap. The floating rate of interest is LIBOR plus 20 basis points. Instead of being paid, the interest is compounded forward until the end of the life of the swap at a rate of LIBOR plus 10 basis points. The fixed rate of interest is 6%. Instead of being paid this interest is compounded forward at a fixed rate of interest of 6.3% until the end of the swap.

The "assume forward rates are realized" approach can be used at least approximately for valuing a compounding swap such as that in Business Snapshot 33.2. It is straightforward to deal with the fixed side of the swap because the payment that will be made at maturity is known with certainty. The "assume forward rates are realized" approach for the floating side is justifiable because there exist a series of forward rate agreements (FRAs) where the floating-rate cash flows are exchanged for the values they would have if each floating rate equaled the corresponding forward rate.1

Footnote 1: See Technical Note 18 at www.rotman.utoronto.ca/~hull/TechnicalNotes for the details. The “assume forward rates are realized” approach works exactly if the spread used for compounding, \(s_{c}\), is zero or if it is applied so that \(Q\) at time \(t\) compounds to \(Q(1+R\tau)(1+s_{c}\tau)\) at time \(t+\tau\), where \(R\) is LIBOR. If, as is more usual, it compounds to \(Q[1+(R+s_{c}\tau)t]\), then there is a small approximation.

question: The concept of the minimum variance hedge ratio is being considered.If there is no basis risk, the minimum variance hedge ratio is less than 1.0.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Minimum variance hedge ratio
Definition: The minimum variance hedge ratio depends on the relationship between changes in the spot price and changes in the futures price. Define:

\(\Delta S\): Change in spot price, \(S\), during a period of time equal to the life of the hedge \(\Delta F\): Change in futures price, \(F\), during a period of time equal to the life of the hedge.

We will denote the minimum variance hedge ratio by \(h^{*}\). It can be shown that \(h^{*}\) is the slope of the best-fit line from a linear regression of \(\Delta S\) against \(\Delta F\) (see Figure 3.2). This result is intuitively reasonable. We would expect \(h^{*}\) to be the ratio of the average change in \(S\) for a particular change in \(F\).

The formula for \(h^{*}\) is:

\[h^{*}=\rho\frac{\sigma_{S}}{\sigma_{F}} \tag{3.1}\]

where \(\sigma_{S}\) is the standard deviation of \(\Delta S\), \(\sigma_{F}\) is the standard deviation of \(\Delta F\), and \(\rho\) is the coefficient of correlation between the two.

Equation (3.1) shows that the optimal hedge ratio is the product of the coefficient of correlation between \(\Delta S\) and \(\Delta F\) and the ratio of the standard deviation of \(\Delta S\) to the standard deviation of \(\Delta F\). Figure 3.3 shows how the variance of the value of the hedger's position depends on the hedge ratio chosen.

If \(\rho=1\) and \(\sigma_{F}=\sigma_{S}\), the hedge ratio, \(h^{*}\), is 1.0. This result is to be expected, because in this case the futures price mirrors the spot price perfectly. If \(\rho=1\) and \(\sigma_{F}=2\sigma_{S}\), the hedge ratio h^{*} is 0.5. This result is also as expected, because in this case the futures price always changes by twice as much as the spot price. 
The parameters ho, \sigma_{F}, and \sigma_{S} in equation (3.1) are usually estimated from historical data on \Delta S and \Delta F. (The implicit assumption is that the future will in some sense be like the past.) A number of equal nonoverlapping time intervals are chosen, and the values of \Delta S and \Delta F for each of the intervals are observed. Ideally, the length of each time interval is the same as the length of the time interval for which the hedge is in effect. In practice, this sometimes severely limits the number of observations that are available, and a shorter time interval is used.

question: A European call and put option have the same strike price and time to maturity. The call has an implied volatility of 30% and the put has an implied volatility of 25%.The correct trading strategy is to sell the put, sell the stock, and buy the call.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: volatility smile and,Greek letters Greeks
Definition: The volatility smile complicates the calculation of Greek letters. Assume that the relationship between the implied volatility and \(K/S\) for an option with a certain time to maturity remains the same.6 As the price of the underlying asset changes, the implied volatility of the option changes to reflect the option's "moneyness" (i.e., the extent to which it is in or out of the money). The formulas for Greek letters given in Chapter 19 are no longer correct. For example, the delta of a call option is given by 

\[\frac{\partial c_{\text{BS}}}{\partial S}+\frac{\partial c_{\text{BS}}}{ \partial\sigma_{\text{imp}}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{\text{imp}}}{\partial S}\]

where \(c_{\text{BS}}\) is the Black-Scholes price of the option expressed as a function of the asset price \(S\) and the implied volatility \(\sigma_{\text{imp}}\). Consider the impact of this formula on the delta of an equity call option. Volatility is a decreasing function of \(K/S\). This means that the implied volatility increases as the asset price increases, so that

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\text{imp}}}{\partial S}>0\]

As a result, delta is higher than that given by the Black-Scholes-Merton assumptions. In practice, banks try to ensure that their exposure to the most commonly observed changes in the volatility surface is reasonably small.

question: One option a firm usually has with any excess cash is to pay its suppliers more quickly.A potential advantage of paying suppliers more quickly is that it decreases the firm's cash cycle.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: costs of holding cash,reasons for holding,Cash
Definition: When a firm holds cash in excess of some necessary minimum, it incurs an opportunity cost. The opportunity cost of excess cash (held in currency or bank deposits) is the interest income that could be earned in the next best use, such as investment in marketable securities.

Given the opportunity cost of holding cash, why would a firm hold cash in excess of its compensating balance requirements? The answer is that a cash balance must be maintained to provide the liquidity necessary for transaction needs--paying bills. If the firm maintains too small a cash balance, it may run out of cash. If this happens, the firm may have to raise cash on a short-term basis. This could involve, for example, selling marketable securities or borrowing.

Activities such as selling marketable securities and borrowing involve various costs. As we've discussed, holding cash has an opportunity cost. To determine the appropriate cash balance, the firm must weigh the benefits of holding cash against these costs. We discuss this subject in more detail in the sections that follow.

question: Consider the payoff from a portfolio consisting of a floating lookback call and a floating lookback put with the same maturity.A floating lookback call provides a payoff of \(S_{\max}-S_{T}\).
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Floating lookback option
Definition: Lookback options are financial derivatives where payoffs are contingent on the maximum or minimum asset price reached during the options' lifetime. A floating lookback call pays off the difference between the final asset price and the minimum price during the option's life, while a floating lookback put pays off the difference between the maximum price during the lifetime and the final asset price.

The value of a floating lookback call at time zero is given by:

\[
c_{\text{fl}}=S_{0}e^{-qT}N(a_{1})-S_{0}e^{-qT}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2(r-q)}N(-a_{1})-S_{\min}e^{-rT}\bigg{[}N(a_{2})-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2(r-q)}e^{Y_{1}}N(-a_{3})\bigg{]}
\]

where:

\[
a_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/S_{\min})+(r-q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]
\[
a_{2} = a_{1}-\sigma\sqrt{T},
\]
\[
a_{3} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/S_{\min})+(-r+q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]
\[
Y_{1} = -\frac{2(r-q-\sigma^{2}/2)\ln(S_{0}/S_{\min})}{\sigma^{2}}
\]

In this context, \(S_{\min}\) is the minimum asset price reached by the option. If the lookback option is just originated, then \(S_{\min}=S_{0}\).

The value of a floating lookback put is expressed as:

\[
p_{\rm fl}=S_{\rm max}e^{-rT}\bigg{[}N(b_{1})-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2(r-q)}e^{Y_{2}}N(-b_{3})\bigg{]}+S_{0}e^{-qT}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2(r-q)}N(-b_{2})-S_{0}e^{-qT}N(b_{2})
\]

where:

\[
b_{1}=\frac{\ln(S_{\rm max}/S_{0})+(-r+q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},
\]
\[
b_{2}=b_{1}-\sigma\sqrt{T},
\]
\[
b_{3}=\frac{\ln(S_{\rm max}/S_{0})+(r-q-\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]
\[
Y_{2}=\frac{2(r-q-\sigma^{2}/2)\ln(S_{\rm max}/S_{0})}{\sigma^{2}}
\]

Here, \(S_{\rm max}\) is the maximum asset price reached by the option, and if just originated, then \(S_{\rm max}=S_{0}\).

A floating lookback call allows the holder to purchase the underlying asset at the lowest price achieved during the option's existence, while a floating lookback put enables the holder to sell the underlying asset at the highest price obtained throughout the option's period.

question: Both Keynes' and Friedman's theories of the demand for money suggest that as the relative expected return on money falls, demand for it will fall.Keynes believed that a rise in interest rates leads to a lower relative expected return of money and consequently a lower demand for money.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money,Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money
Definition: The theory of asset demand suggests that the demand for money is influenced by individual wealth and the expected returns of other assets compared to the expected return on money. Friedman formulated the demand for money as follows:

\[
\frac{M^{d}}{P} = f(Y_{p}, r_{b}-r_{m}, r_{e}-r_{m}, \pi^{e}-r_{m})
\]

where:
- \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) = demand for real money balances
- \(Y_{p}\) = Friedman's measure of wealth, known as permanent income
- \(r_{m}\) = expected return on money
- \(r_{b}\) = expected return on bonds
- \(r_{e}\) = expected return on equity (common stocks)
- \(\pi^{e}\) = expected inflation rate

The demand for money \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) is positively related to permanent income \(Y_{p}\) while negatively related to the terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\), \(r_{e}-r_{m}\), and \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\). 

Permanent income is the present discounted value of expected future income, representing a long-term average that minimizes fluctuations from short-run income changes. As such, the demand for money, influenced by permanent income, remains relatively stable despite business cycle fluctuations. 

Individuals can hold wealth in several forms, categorized by Friedman into three types of assets: bonds, equity, and goods. The demand for these assets relative to money is shaped by expected returns, reflected in the latter terms of the demand function. 

The expected return on money \(r_{m}\) is determined by two factors: the services provided by banks on deposits, such as check provision or bill payments, and interest payments on money balances. An increase in either of these factors generally raises the expected return on holding money.

The terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\) and \(r_{e}-r_{m}\) compare the expected returns on bonds and equity, respectively, to money. As these terms increase, the relative attractiveness of money diminishes, leading to a decreased demand for money. Additionally, the term \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\) compares the expected return on goods (driven by capital gains from price increases, reflecting inflation) to money. An increase in this term indicates that holding goods becomes more attractive compared to money, which also results in a decreased demand for money.

Overall, Friedman's model illustrates the dynamic interplay between wealth, asset returns, and the demand for money, emphasizing the stability of money demand during economic fluctuations while highlighting how relative returns on various assets influence money-holding behaviors.

question: Interest rates tend to increase when aggregate output increases during a boom and tend to fall when aggregate output falls during a recession.When output rises and interest rates rise, banks would increase the level of their excess reserves, leading to a fall in the money supply.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Traditional Interest-Rate Channels,Transmission Mechanisms of Monetary Policy
Definition: The traditional view of the monetary transmission mechanism illustrates how expansionary monetary policy impacts the economy through a schematic representation: 

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow i_{t} \downarrow \Rightarrow l \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

An expansionary monetary policy results in a decrease in real interest rates (i_t, \downarrow), which lowers the cost of capital, thus increasing investment spending (l \uparrow) and boosting aggregate demand, leading to a rise in output (Y \uparrow). 

While Keynes highlighted the significance of businesses’ investment decisions, the exploration of monetary transmission channels recognized that consumer spending, particularly on housing and consumer durables (like cars and refrigerators), also qualifies as investment. Thus, the interest-rate channel applies to consumer expenditure as well.

A crucial aspect of this interest-rate transmission mechanism is its focus on real interest rates rather than nominal rates. Typically, the real long-term interest rate, rather than the short-term rate, has a more substantial effect on spending. When central banks adjust short-term nominal interest rates, it influences real interest rates across both short- and long-term bonds. This connection stems from the concept of _sticky prices_, indicating that aggregate price levels change slowly. Hence, a drop in short-term nominal rates from expansionary monetary policy also leads to lower short-term real interest rates. The expectations hypothesis of the term structure states that the long-term interest rate reflects an average of expected future short-term rates, meaning a persistent reduction in real short-term rates decreases the real long-term rate as well. Lower real interest rates then contribute to increases in business fixed investment, residential housing investment, inventory investment, and consumer durable expenditure, resulting in a rise in aggregate output.

The importance of real interest rates over nominal rates in driving spending highlights a mechanism through which monetary policy can stimulate the economy, even during deflationary periods. When nominal interest rates reach a zero floor, a commitment to future expansionary monetary policy can lead to higher expected price levels (P^{e} \uparrow) and expected inflation (\pi^{e} \uparrow). Consequently, this lowers the real interest rate (i_{r} = [i - \pi^{e}] \downarrow) despite nominal rates remaining fixed at zero, stimulating spending through the interest-rate channel:

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow P^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow \pi^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow i_{r} \downarrow \Rightarrow I \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

This mechanism illustrates that monetary policy can remain effective even when nominal rates are constrained to zero. It also sheds light on monetarist views regarding the U.S. economy's ability to avoid a liquidity trap during the Great Depression, suggesting that expansionary monetary policy could have mitigated the sharp output decline experienced during that time.

When nominal interest rates reach a zero floor, a commitment to future expansionary monetary policy can lead to higher expected price levels (P^{e} \uparrow) and expected inflation (\pi^{e} \uparrow). Consequently, this lowers the real interest rate (i_{r} = [i - \pi^{e}] \downarrow) despite nominal rates remaining fixed at zero, stimulating spending through the interest-rate channel:

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow P^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow \pi^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow i_{r} \downarrow \Rightarrow I \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

This mechanism illustrates that monetary policy can remain effective even when nominal rates are constrained to zero. It also sheds light on monetarist views regarding the U.S. economy's ability to avoid a liquidity trap during the Great Depression, suggesting that expansionary monetary policy could have mitigated the sharp output decline experienced during that time.

question: A corporate treasurer has negotiated a five-year loan at a competitive fixed rate of interest of 5.2%. He achieved this rate by borrowing at six-month LIBOR plus 150 basis points and swapping LIBOR for 3.7%, believing his company has a comparative advantage in the floating-rate market.If the treasurer's spread over LIBOR increases from 150 basis points to 200 basis points, the borrowing rate will still remain at 5.2%.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: comparative-advantage argument,Interest rate swap
Definition: Swaps, especially interest rate swaps, gain popularity from the principle of comparative advantage. Companies may possess distinct advantages when borrowing in fixed versus floating-rate markets. Thus, a firm may choose to borrow at fixed rates when it desires floating rates, or vice versa. For instance, consider AAACorp and BBBCorp, both seeking to borrow $10 million for 5 years, where AAACorp (AAA rated) prefers floating rates linked to 6-month LIBOR, while BBBCorp (BBB rated) opts for fixed rates.

BBBCorp faces higher interest rates than AAACorp due to its credit rating, with BBBCorp's fixed-rate being 1.2% higher than AAACorp's, compared to a 0.7% differential in floating rates. This anomaly leads to a potential swap arrangement where AAACorp borrows at a fixed rate of 4% per annum and BBBCorp at LIBOR + 0.6%. They create a swap agreement whereby AAACorp pays BBBCorp interest at 6-month LIBOR for $10 million, and in return, BBBCorp pays AAACorp a fixed rate of 4.35% per annum.

The cash flows for AAACorp are:
1. Pays 4% per annum to outside lenders.
2. Receives 4.35% from BBBCorp.
3. Pays LIBOR to BBBCorp.
The net effect for AAACorp is LIBOR - 0.35% per annum, 0.25% lower than if it accessed floating-rate markets directly.

For BBBCorp:
1. Pays LIBOR + 0.6% to outside lenders.
2. Receives LIBOR from AAACorp.
3. Pays 4.35% to AAACorp.
The net effect results in BBBCorp paying 4.95%, also 0.25% lower than if borrowing directly at fixed rates. In this arrangement, both companies realize the same gain, 0.25%. The overall gain from the interest rate swap is represented as \(a - b\), where \(a\) is the spread in fixed-rate markets (1.2%) and \(b\) in floating-rate markets (0.7%), yielding a total gain of 0.5%.

If facilitated through a financial institution, metrics shift slightly: AAACorp borrows at LIBOR - 0.33%, BBBCorp at 4.97%, and the intermediary earns a spread of 4 basis points, leading to gains of 0.23% each for AAACorp and BBBCorp, and 0.04% for the financial institution, preserving the total gain of 0.5%.

Skepticism arises around why spreads differ between fixed and floating markets. The disparity is attributed to the nature of contracts; the fixed rates (like 4.0% and 5.2% for AAACorp and BBBCorp) are for 5-year terms, while floating rates (LIBOR - 0.1% and LIBOR + 0.6%) are 6-month rates. Floating-rate lenders can reassess terms every 6 months based on creditworthiness changes, unlike fixed-rate providers. Hence, the spread between the rates mirrors the expected likelihood of default, with BBBCorp's risk climbing as time progresses.

Post-swap, while BBBCorp may seem to secure a fixed loan at 4.97%, the actual cost hinges on BBBCorp's future creditworthiness and associated spreads. If BBBCorp's credit deteriorates, its borrowing may rise significantly, impacting the swap's perceived benefits. AAACorp, meanwhile, can lock in its LIBOR - 0.33% rate for five years but incurs the risk tied to potential defaults by the financial institution, a risk mitigated had it borrowed through conventional means.

\centering
\caption{Borrowing rates that provide a basis for the comparative-advantage argument.}
\begin{tabular}{|l|c|c|}
\hline
 & Fixed & Floating \\ \hline
AAACorp & 4.0\% & 6-month LIBOR - 0.1\% \\ \hline
BBBCorp & 5.2\% & 6-month LIBOR + 0.6\% \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: effect on VaR estimates,Gamma
Definition: The application of linear models to portfolios that include options is considered, starting with a portfolio of options on a single stock priced at S. The delta of the position, denoted as \(\delta\), reflects the rate of change of the portfolio value with respect to stock price, formulated as:

\[
\delta=\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta S}
\]
or equivalently,

\[
\Delta P=\delta\,\Delta S
\]

Here, \(\Delta S\) represents the dollar change in stock price over one day. Let \(\Delta x\) denote the percentage change in stock price:

\[
\Delta x=\frac{\Delta S}{S}
\]

From this, an approximate relationship between \(\Delta P\) and \(\Delta x\) can be established:

\[
\Delta P=S\delta\,\Delta x
\]

In scenarios with multiple underlying market variables that involve options, a linear approximation gives:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}
\]

where \(S_{i}\) is the value of the ith market variable and \(\delta_{i}\) is the delta of the portfolio related to that variable. This leads to the use of equations (22.1) for calculating the standard deviation of \(\Delta P\).

The linear model serves as an approximation and does not factor in the gamma of the portfolio, which measures the curvature of the relationship between portfolio value and underlying market variables. Gamma is defined as the rate of change of delta with respect to the market variable. Positive gamma portfolios result in positively skewed probability distributions, while negative gamma portfolios result in negatively skewed distributions.

The Value at Risk (VaR) for a portfolio is sensitive to the left tail of its probability distribution. For a 99% confidence level, the VaR represents the value below which 1% of the distribution lies. Positive gamma portfolios generally have a lighter left tail compared to normal distributions, leading to overestimation of VaR. Conversely, negative gamma portfolios typically exhibit a heavier left tail, resulting in underestimation of VaR.

For a more precise VaR estimate, both delta and gamma should relate \(\Delta P\) to \(\Delta x_{i}\). For a portfolio linked to a single asset, the relationship is expressed as:

\[
\Delta P=\delta\,\Delta S+\tfrac{1}{2}\gamma(\Delta S)^{2}
\]

With the substitution \(\Delta x=\frac{\Delta S}{S}\), it simplifies to:

\[
\Delta P=S\delta\,\Delta x+\tfrac{1}{2}S^{2}\gamma(\Delta x)^{2}
\]

For portfolios with n underlying market variables, the equation expands to:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{1}{2} S_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}\,(\Delta x_{i})^{2}
\]

where \(\delta_{i}\) and \(\gamma_{i}\) are the delta and gamma with respect to the ith market variable. In cases where individual instruments depend on multiple variables, the equation takes the form:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}S_{i}S_{j}\gamma_{ij}\,\Delta x_{i}\,\Delta x_{j}
\]

with the "cross gamma" defined as:

\[
\gamma_{ij}=\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial S_{i}\,\partial S_{j}}
\]

While equation (22.7) is more complex, it provides a means to calculate moments for \(\Delta P\). The Cornish-Fisher expansion can subsequently estimate the percentiles of the probability distribution based on those moments.

question: Consider the pricing of an at-the-money European call futures option and a similar at-the-money European put futures option.The price of an at-the-money European call futures option is always different from the price of a similar at-the-money European put futures option.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: put–call parity,Futures option
Definition: The put-call parity relationship for European futures options can be derived through two distinct portfolios. 

**Portfolio A** consists of a European call futures option plus cash equal to \(Ke^{-rT}\). The call option can be exercised at maturity, resulting in the value of this portfolio at time \(T\) being:

\[
\max(F_{T},\ K)
\]

**Portfolio B** includes a European put futures option, a long futures contract, and cash equal to \(F_{0}e^{-rT}\) (where \(F_{0}\) is the futures price). At time \(T\), portfolio B's value is given by:

\[
F_{0} + (F_{T} - F_{0}) + \max(K - F_{T}, 0) = \max(F_{T},\ K)
\]

Since both portfolios exhibit equivalent value at time \(T\) and European options cannot be exercised early, their present values must also be equal. The value of portfolio A now is:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT}
\]

where \(c\) is the price of the call futures option. In contrast, due to daily settlement, portfolio B's current value is:

\[
p + F_{0}e^{-rT}
\]

where \(p\) pertains to the price of the put futures option. Thus, the put-call parity relationship is established as:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = p + F_{0}e^{-rT} \tag{18.1}
\]

In contrast to non-dividend-paying stock options, the stock price \(S_{0}\) is substituted by the discounted futures price \(F_{0}e^{-rT}\).

For American futures options, the relationship is represented as:

\[
F_{0}e^{-rT} - K < C - P < F_{0} - Ke^{-rT}
\]

The put-call parity relationship in equation (18.1) also delineates bounds for European call and put options. Given that the price of a put option \(p\) cannot be negative, it leads to:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} \geq F_{0}e^{-rT} 
\]

and thus,

\[
c \geq \max((F_{0} - K)e^{-rT}, 0)
\]

Conversely, since the price of a call option \(c\) cannot be negative, it follows:

\[
Ke^{-rT} \leq F_{0}e^{-rT} + p 
\]

resulting in:

\[
p \geq \max((K - F_{0})e^{-rT}, 0)
\]

These bounds are akin to those for European stock options. When options are deep in the money, the prices of European call and put options approach their lower bounds. For deep in-the-money call options, the associated put options become deep out of the money, causing \(p\) to approach zero, and consequently the difference between call price \(c\) and its lower bound mirrors \(p\). A similar logic applies to put options.

As American futures options can be exercised at any moment, it holds that:

\[
C \geq \max(F_{0} - K, 0) 
\]

and 

\[
C \geq \max(K - F_{0}, 0)
\]

Thus, assuming positive interest rates, the lower boundary for an American option price exceeds that of its corresponding European option price, as early exercise remains a potential advantage.

question: The cost of equity does not involve the same tax considerations as debt.There is no difference between pretax and aftertax equity costs.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: tax,Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
Definition: There is one final issue we need to discuss. Recall that we are always concerned with aftertax cash flows. If we are determining the discount rate appropriate to those cash flows, then the discount rate also needs to be expressed on an aftertax basis.

As we discussed previously in various places in this book (and as we will discuss later), the interest paid by a corporation is deductible for tax purposes. Payments to stockholders, such as dividends, are not. What this means, effectively, is that the government pays some of the interest. Thus, in determining an aftertax discount rate, we need to distinguish between the pretax and the aftertax cost of debt.

To illustrate, suppose a firm borrows S1 million at 9 percent interest. The corporate tax rate is 34 percent. What is the aftertax interest rate on this loan? The total interest bill will be S90,000 per year. This amount is tax deductible, however, so the S90,000 interest reduces the firm's tax bill by .34 x $90,000 = $30,600. The aftertax interest bill is thus S90,000 - 30,600 = S59,400. The aftertax interest rate is thus S59,400/1 million = 5.94%.

Notice that, in general, the aftertax interest rate is simply equal to the pretax rate multiplied by 1 minus the tax rate. If we use the symbol \(T_{c}\) to stand for the corporate tax rate, then the aftertax rate can be written as \(R_{o}\times(1-T_{C})\). For example, using the numbers from the preceding paragraph, we find that the aftertax interest rate is \(9\%\times(1-.34)=5.94\%\).

Bringing together the various topics we have discussed in this chapter, we now have the capital structure weights along with the cost of equity and the aftertax cost of debt. To calculate the firm's overall cost of capital, we multiply the capital structure weights by the associated costs and add them up. The total is the **weighted average cost of capital (WACC)**:

\[\text{WACC} = (E/V) \times R_{E} + (D/V) \times R_{b} \times (1-T_{C})\]

This WACC has a straightforward interpretation. It is the overall return the firm must earn on its existing assets to maintain the value of its stock. It is also the required return on any investments by the firm that have essentially the same risks as existing operations. So, if we were evaluating the cash flows from a proposed expansion of our existing operations, this is the discount rate we would use.

If a firm uses preferred stock in its capital structure, then our expression for the WACC needs a simple extension. If we define \(P/V\) as the percentage of the firm's financing that comes from preferred stock, then the WACC is simply:

\[\text{WACC} = (E/V) \times R_{E} + (P/V) \times R_{P} + (D/V) \times R_{b} \times (1-T_{C})\]

where \(R_{P}\) is the cost of preferred stock.

question: When discussing the behavior of the economy in relation to the IS and LM curves.The economy comes to rest only when it is at the intersection of both the IS and LM curves, as there is no tendency for the interest rate and output to change at this point.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: ISLM Model,ISLM Approach to Aggregate Output and Interest Rates
Definition: Now that we have derived the IS and LM curves, we can put them into the same diagram (Figure 9) to produce a model that enables us to determine both aggregate output and the interest rate. The only point at which the goods market and the market for money are in simultaneous equilibrium is at the intersection of the IS and LM curves, point E. At this point, aggregate output equals aggregate demand (IS) and the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity of money supplied (LM). At any other point in the diagram, at least one of these equilibrium conditions is not satisfied, and market forces move the economy toward the general equilibrium, point E.
To learn how this works, lets consider what happens if the economy is at point A, which is on the IS curve but not the LM curve. Even though at point A the goods market is in equilibrium, so that aggregate output equals aggregate demand, the interest rate is above its equilibrium level, so the demand for money is less than the supply. Because people have more money than they want to hold, they will try to get rid of it by buying bonds. The resulting rise in bond prices causes a fall in interest rates, which in turn causes both planned investment spending and net exports to rise, and thus aggregate output rises. The economy then moves down along the IS curve, and the process continues until the interest rate falls to i* and aggregate output rises to Y*--that is, until the economy is at equilibrium point E.
If the economy is on the LM curve but off the IS curve at point B, it will also head toward the equilibrium at point E. At point B, even though money demand equals money supply, output is higher than the equilibrium level and exceeds aggregate demand. Firms are unable to sell all their output, and unplanned inventory accumulates, prompting firms to cut production and lower output. The decline in output means that the demand for money will fall, lowering interest rates. The economy then moves down along the LM curve until it reaches equilibrium point E.
We have finally developed a model, the ISLM model, that tells us how both interest rates and aggregate output are determined when the price level is fixed. Although we have demonstrated that the economy will head toward an aggregate output level of Y*, there is no reason to assume that at this level of aggregate output the economy is at full employment. If the unemployment rate is too high, government policymakers might want to increase aggregate output to reduce it. The ISLM apparatus indicates that they can do this by manipulating monetary and fiscal policy.

Finance term: policy instrument,Tactics: Choosing the Policy Instrument
Definition: The **policy instrument** (also called an **operating instrument**) is a variable that responds to the central banks tools and indicates the stance (easy or tight) of monetary policy. A central bank like the Fed has at its disposal two basic types of policy instruments: reserve aggregates (total reserves, nonborrowed reserves, the monetary base, and the nonborrowed base) and interest rates (federal funds rate and other short-term interest rates). 
The policy instrument might be linked to an **intermediate target**, such as a monetary aggregate like M2 or a long-term interest rate. Intermediate targets stand between the policy instrument and the goals of monetary policy (e.g., price stability, output growth); they are not as directly affected by the tools of monetary policy, but might be more closely linked to the goals of monetary policy. As a study aid, Figure 2 shows a schematic of the linkages between the tools of monetary policy, policy instruments, intermediate targets, and the goals of monetary policy. 
As an example, suppose the central banks employment and inflation goals are consistent with a nominal GDP growth rate of 5%. The central bank might believe that the 5% nominal GDP growth rate will be achieved by a 4% growth rate for M2 (an intermediate target), which will in turn be achieved by a growth rate of 3% for nonborrowed reserves (the policy instrument). Alternatively, the central bank might believe that the best way to achieve its objectives would be to set the federal funds rate (a policy instrument) at, say, 4%. Can the central bank choose to target both the nonborrowed-reserves and the federal-funds-rate policy instruments at the same time? The answer is no. The application of supply and demand analysis to the market for reserves we developed in Chapter 15 explains why a central bank must choose one or the other.

question: A bank uses Black's model to price European bond options.Using the implied price volatility for a five-year option on a ten-year bond to price a nine-year option on the bond would result in a price that is too high.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: European,Bond option
Definition: Many over-the-counter and some embedded bond options are European, where the standard market model assumes the forward bond price has a volatility \\(\\sigma_{B}\\). This allows the application of Black's model for valuation. The equations for European bond options are:

\[
c = P(0,T)[F_{B}N(d_{1})-KN(d_{2})] \tag{29.1}
\] 
\[
p = P(0,T)[KN(-d_{2})-F_{B}N(-d_{1})] \tag{29.2}
\] 

In these equations, \\(K\\) represents the strike price, \\(T\\) the time to maturity, and \\(P(0,T)\\) the risk-free discount factor. The terms \\(d_{1}\\) and \\(d_{2}\\) are defined as:

\[
d_{1}=\frac{\ln(F_{B}/K)+\sigma_{B}^{2}T/2}{\sigma_{B}\sqrt{T}} \quad \text{and} \quad d_{2}=d_{1}-\sigma_{B}\sqrt{T}
\]

The forward bond price \\(F_{B}\\) can be computed using:

\[
F_{B}=\frac{B_{0}-I}{P(0,T)} \tag{29.3}
\]

Here, \\(B_{0}\\) is the bond price at time zero, and \\(I\\) is the present value of the coupons during the option's life. Both \\(F_{B}\\) and \\(B_{0}\\) are expressed as cash prices, with a distinction between cash and quoted prices elaborated in Section 6.1. 

The strike price \\(K\\) should be set based on the cash amount exchanged for the bond. If the strike price is defined as the quoted price in the option exercise, then \\(K\\) would equal this quoted price plus accrued interest at expiration. Traders refer to the quoted price as the "clean price" and the cash price as the "dirty price."

The volatility relevant for valuing a European option on the bond is given by:

\[
\frac{\text{Standard deviation of logarithm of bond price at maturity of option}}{\sqrt{\text{Time to maturity of option}}}
\]

As the life of the option increases, the volatility \\(\\sigma_{B}\\) typically shows a declining pattern, as illustrated in Figure 29.2, contrasting with how the standard deviation of a bond's price evolves over time, peaking between today and the bond's maturity. Figure 29.1 depicts that the standard deviation is zero today (due to no uncertainty about the current price) and also zero at maturity (where the bond's price equals its face value).
