Finance term: valuation of,Currency swap
Definition: Like interest rate swaps, fixed-for-fixed currency swaps can be decomposed into either the difference between two bonds or a portfolio of forward contracts.

### Valuation in Terms of Bond Prices

If we define \(V_{\text{swap}}\) as the value in US dollars of an outstanding swap where dollars are received and a foreign currency is paid, then

\[V_{\text{swap}}=B_{D}-S_{0}B_{F}\]

where \(B_{F}\) is the value, measured in the foreign currency, of the bond defined by the foreign cash flows on the swap and \(B_{D}\) is the value of the bond defined by the domestic cash flows on the swap, and \(S_{0}\) is the spot exchange rate (expressed as number of dollars per unit of foreign currency). The value of a swap can therefore be determined from interest rates in the two currencies and the spot exchange rate.

Similarly, the value of a swap where the foreign currency is received and dollars are paid is

\[V_{\text{swap}}=S_{0}B_{F}-B_{D}\]

### Valuation as Portfolio of Forward Contracts

Each exchange of payments in a fixed-for-fixed currency swap is a forward foreign exchange contract. In Section 5.7, forward foreign exchange contracts were valued by assuming that forward exchange rates are realized. The same assumption can therefore be made for a currency swap.

The value of a currency swap is normally close to zero initially. If the two principals are worth the same at the start of the swap, the value of the swap is also close to zero immediately after the initial exchange of principal. However, as in the case of interest rate swaps, this does not mean that each of the individual forward contracts underlying the swap has a value close to zero. It can be shown that, when interest rates in two currencies are significantly different, the payer of the currency with the high interest rate is in the position where the forward contracts corresponding to the early exchanges of cash flows have negative values, and the forward contract corresponding to final exchange of principals has a positive value. The payer of the currency with the low interest rate is in the opposite position; that is, the forward contracts corresponding to the early exchanges of cash flows have positive values, while that corresponding to the final exchange has a negative value. These results are important when the credit risk in the swap is being evaluated.

data.content:
Finance term: put-call parity,European option
Definition: An important relationship between the prices of European put and call options with the same strike price \\(K\\) and time to maturity \\(T\\) is derived using two portfolios:

- **Portfolio A** consists of one European call option and a zero-coupon bond with a payoff of \\(K\\) at time \\(T\\).
- **Portfolio C** includes one European put option and one share of the stock.

Assuming the stock pays no dividends, at time \\(T\\), the value of Portfolio A can be either \\(S_{T}\\) if \\(S_{T} > K\\) (the call is exercised) or \\(K\\) if \\(S_{T} < K\\) (the call expires worthless). Conversely, Portfolio C's value at time \\(T\\) will also be \\(K\\) if \\(S_{T} < K\\) (the put is exercised) or \\(S_{T}\\) if \\(S_{T} > K\\) (the put expires worthless). Thus, both portfolios provide the same final value:

\[
\max(S_{T}, K)
\]

Due to the identical values at expiration, the portfolios must have the same present value to prevent arbitrage opportunities. Therefore, it follows that:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_{0} \tag{11.6}
\]

This is known as **put-call parity**, establishing a relationship between the prices of European call and put options.

To illustrate arbitrage opportunities, consider a scenario where the stock price \\(S_{0} = 31\\), exercise price \\(K = 30\\), risk-free interest rate \\(r = 10\%\\), call price \\(c = 3\\), and put price \\(p = 2.25\\). The values yield:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = 3 + 30e^{-0.1 \times 3/12} = \$32.26
\]
\[
p + S_{0} = 2.25 + 31 = \$33.25
\]

In this case, Portfolio C is overpriced. An arbitrageur could buy Portfolio A and short Portfolio C to lock in a profit, generating an upfront cash flow of:

\[
-3 + 2.25 + 31 = \$30.25
\]

Investing this amount at the risk-free rate results in:

\[
30.25e^{0.1 \times 0.25} = \$31.02
\]

Regardless of whether the call or put is exercised upon expiration, the arbitrageur ends up buying one share for \$30, resulting in a net profit of:

\[
\$31.02 - \$30.00 = \$1.02
\]

Conversely, if the call price is \\(c = 3\\) and put price is \\(p = 1\\), a different situation arises:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = 3 + 30e^{-0.1 \times 3/12} = \$32.26
\]
\[
p + S_{0} = 1 + 31 = \$32.00
\]

This indicates Portfolio A is overpriced relative to Portfolio C. An arbitrageur can short Portfolio A and buy Portfolio C, resulting in an initial investment of:

\[
31 + 1 - 3 = \$29
\]

When this is financed at the risk-free rate, repayment requires:

\[
29e^{0.1 \times 0.25} = \$29.73
\]

The final profit is:

\[
\$30.00 - \$29.73 = \$0.27
\]

Additionally, the implied volatility of European call options is shown to be the same as that of European put options when they share the same strike price and maturity date. This result implies that for a specific strike price and maturity, the Black-Scholes-Merton model's volatility is consistent across both types of options, reinforcing that the volatility surface is identical for European calls and puts, and approximately so for American options.
\begin{table}[h]
    \centering
    \caption{Values of Portfolio A and Portfolio C at time $T$.}
    \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
        \hline
        & $S_T > K$ & $S_T < K$ \\ \hline
        Portfolio A & & \\ 
        \quad Call option & $S_T - K$ & 0 \\ 
        \quad Zero-coupon bond & $K$ & $K$ \\ 
        \hline
        Total & $S_T$ & $K$ \\ 
        \hline
        Portfolio C & & \\ 
        \quad Put Option & 0 & $K - S_T$ \\ 
        \quad Share & $S_T$ & $S_T$ \\ 
        \hline
        Total & $S_T$ & $K$ \\ 
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

data.content:
Finance term: values,Bonds
Definition: Just like any financial instrument, bonds are affected by fluctuations in interest rates. As marketplace interest rates change, the cash flows from a bond remain constant, leading to variations in the bond's market value. When interest rates rise, the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows declines, reducing its value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, the bond's value increases.

To accurately assess the value of a bond at any given time, it is crucial to know the following: the number of periods remaining until maturity, the bond's face value, the coupon payments, and the prevailing market interest rate for similar bonds. This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

Finance term: future value of,multiple cash flows,Discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation
Definition: When a deposit of $100 is made today in an account with an 8 percent interest rate, the calculation of its future value involves a second $100 deposit made one year later. By the end of the first year, the account balance is $108 from the first deposit, plus the second $100, totaling $208. This amount, when left on deposit for another year at the same interest rate, grows to:

\[
\$208 \times 1.08 = \$224.64
\]

The process is illustrated through a time line, showing when cash flows occur. The first cash flow of $100 happens at time 0, and the second $100 cash flow occurs at time 1. To compute the future value of both deposits, the balance is calculated at the start of each year and carried forward to the next year.

Alternatively, future values can be calculated more directly. The first $100, deposited for two years at 8 percent, results in:

\[
\text{$100} \times 1.08^{2} = \text{$100} \times 1.1664 = \text{$116.64}
\]

The second $100, which is deposited for only one year, yields:

\[
\text{$100} \times 1.08 = \text{$108}
\]

Summing these results:

\[
\$116.64 + \$108 = \$224.64
\]

Thus, both methods yield the same total future value.

Further illustrating future value calculations, consider an example of investing $2,000 at the end of each of the next five years, with a current balance of zero and an interest rate of 10 percent. A time line approach reveals that the first investment earns interest for four years, while the last $2,000, made at the end of the fifth year, earns no interest.

When compounding the investment one period at a time, the future value amounts to $12,210.20. This demonstrates two established methods for calculating future values: compounding the accumulated balance year by year or calculating the future value of each cash flow individually and summing them. Both approaches yield consistent results.

Finance term: with multiple cash flows,Present value (PV)
Definition: Determining the present value of future cash flows can be approached in two primary ways: discounting each cash flow one period at a time or calculating each present value individually and summing them.

For example, to find out how much money to invest today to obtain $1,000 in one year and $2,000 in two years at a 9% return, we calculate the present value of each cash flow:

1. The present value of $2,000 in two years at 9%:
   \[
   \text{PV} = \frac{\text{$2,000}}{1.09^{2}} = \text{$1,683.36}
   \]

2. The present value of $1,000 in one year:
   \[
   \text{PV} = \frac{\text{$1,000}}{1.09} = \text{$917.43}
   \]

Adding these amounts gives the total present value:
\[
\text{Total PV} = \text{$1,683.36} + \text{$917.43} = \text{$2,600.79}
\]

To verify this amount, if $2,600.79 is invested today at 9%, the future values can be calculated as follows: after one year, it grows to:
\[
\text{$2,600.79} \times 1.09 = \text{$2,834.86}
\]
Subtracting the $1,000 needed after one year leaves:
\[
\text{$2,834.86} - \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,834.86}
\]
In the second year, this amount further accrues interest:
\[
\text{$1,834.86} \times 1.09 = \text{$2,000}
\]
This checks out according to the planned future cash flows.

An alternative method of calculating present values for recurring cash flows, such as receiving $1,000 at the end of each year for five years, involves discounting each cash flow separately and summing them. For instance, at a 6% discount rate, the present value is calculated as:
\[
\text{PV} = \sum \frac{\text{$1,000}}{(1.06)^t} \quad (t = 1 \text{ to } 5)
\]

In another approach, you can recursively discount cash flows back to the present. For example, starting with the last cash flow:
\[
\text{PV} = \frac{\text{$1,000}}{1.06} + 1,000 = \text{$943.40} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,943.40}
\]
This discounted amount can then be added to the cash flow from the next year, giving:
\[
\frac{\text{$1,943.40}}{1.06} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,833.40} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$2,833.40}
\]

This process of discounting and summing can be repeated for all cash flows until the present value is fully calculated.

Finance term: Butterfly spread,spreads,Trading strategies involving options
Definition: A _butterfly spread_ involves positions in options with three different strike prices. It can be created by buying a European call option with a relatively low strike price \\(K_{1}\\)\n\nbuying a European call option with a relatively high strike price \\(K_{3}\\), and selling two European call options with a strike price \\(K_{2}\\) that is halfway between \\(K_{1}\\) and \\(K_{3}\\). Generally, \\(K_{2}\\) is close to the current stock price. The pattern of profits from the strategy is shown in Figure 12.6. A butterfly spread leads to a profit if the stock price stays close to \\(K_{2}\\), but gives rise to a small loss if there is a significant stock price move in either direction. It is therefore an appropriate strategy for an investor who feels that large stock price moves are unlikely. The strategy requires a small investment initially. The payoff from a butterfly spread is shown in Table 12.4.\n\nSuppose that a certain stock is currently worth $61. Consider an investor who feels that a significant price move in the next 6 months is unlikely. Suppose that the market prices of 6-month European calls are as follows:\n\n\\begin{tabular}{c c} \\hline \\hline _Strike price_ (\\$ ) & Call price (\\$) \\\\ \\hline\n55 & 10 \\\\\n60 & 7 \\\\\n65 & 5 \\\\ \\hline \\hline \\end{tabular} The investor could create a butterfly spread by buying one call with a $55 strike price, buying one call with a $65 strike price, and selling two calls with a $60 strike price. It costs \\(\\$10+\\$5-(2\\times\\$7)=\\$1\\) to create the spread. If the stock price in 6 months is greater than $65 or less than $55, the total payoff is zero, and the investor incurs a net loss of $1. If the stock price is between $56 and $64, a profit is made. The maximum profit, $4, occurs when the stock price in 6 months is $60.\n\nButterfly spreads can be created using put options. The investor buys two European puts, one with a low strike price and one with a high strike price, and sells two European puts with an intermediate strike price, as illustrated in Figure 12.7. The butterfly spread in the example considered above would be created by buying one put with a strike price of $55, another with a strike price of $65, and selling two puts with a strike price of $60. The use of put options results in exactly the same spread as the use of call options. Put-call parity can be used to show that the initial investment is the same in both cases.\n\nA butterfly spread can be sold or shorted by following the reverse strategy. Options are sold with strike prices of \\(K_{1}\\) and \\(K_{3}\\), and two options with the middle strike price \\(K_{2}\\) are purchased. This strategy produces a modest profit if there is a significant movement in the stock price.

        \hline
        Stock price range & Payoff from first long call & Payoff from second long call & Payoff from short calls & Total payoff* \\
        \hline
        $S_T \leq K_1$ & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
        \hline
        $K_1 < S_T \leq K_2$ & $S_T - K_1$ & 0 & 0 & $S_T - K_1$ \\
        \hline

    \end{tabular}

\end{table}

Finance term: erosion and,Incremental cash flows
Definition: Remember that the incremental cash flows for a project include all the resulting changes in the _firm's_ future cash flows. It would not be unusual for a project to have side, or spillover, effects, both good and bad. For example, in 2005, the time between the theatrical release of a feature film and the release of the DVD had shrunk to 137 days compared to 200 days in 1998. This shortened release time was blamed for at least part of the decline in movie theater box office receipts. Of course, retailers cheered the move because it was credited with increasing DVD sales. A negative impact on the cash flows of an existing product from the introduction of a new product is called **erosion**.3 In this case, the cash flows from the new line should be adjusted downward to reflect lost profits on other lines.

Footnote 3: More colorfully, erosion is sometimes called _piracy_ or _cannibalism_.

In accounting for erosion, it is important to recognize that any sales lost as a result of launching a new product might be lost anyway because of future competition. Erosion is relevant only when the sales would not otherwise be lost.

Side effects show up in a lot of different ways. For example, one of Walt Disney Company's concerns when it built Euro Disney was that the new park would drain visitors from the Florida park, a popular vacation destination for Europeans.

There are beneficial spillover effects, of course. For example, you might think that Hewlett-Packard would have been concerned when the price of a printer that sold for $500 to $600 in 1994 declined to below $100 by 2007, but such was not the case. HP realized that the big money is in the consumables that printer owners buy to keep their printers going, such as ink-jet cartridges, laser toner cartridges, and special paper. The profit margins for these products are substantial.

Finance term: valuation binomial tree,Currency option
Definition: When the length of the time step on a binomial tree is \(\Delta t\), we should match volatility by setting

\[u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{13.15}\]

and

\[d=e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{13.16}\]

Also, from equation (13.6),

\[p=\frac{a-d}{u-d} \tag{13.17}\]

where

\[a=e^{r\Delta t} \tag{13.18}\]

Equations (13.15) to (13.18) define the tree.

A foreign currency can be regarded as an asset providing a yield at the foreign risk-free rate of interest, \(r_{f}\). By analogy with the stock index case we can construct a tree for options on a currency by using equations (13.15) to (13.18) and setting \(a=e^{(r-r_{f})\Delta t}\).

Definition: We now move on to consider forward and futures foreign currency contracts from the perspective of a US investor. The underlying asset is one unit of the foreign currency. We will therefore define the variable \\(S_{0}\\) as the current spot price in US dollars of one unit of the foreign currency and \\(F_{0}\\) as the forward or futures price in US dollars of one unit of the foreign currency. This is consistent with the way we have defined \\(S_{0}\\) and \\(F_{0}\\) for other assets underlying forward and futures contracts. However, as mentioned in Section 2.11, it does not necessarily correspond to the way spot and forward exchange rates are quoted. For major exchange rates other than the British pound, euro, Australian dollar, and New Zealand dollar, a spot or forward exchange rate is normally quoted as the number of units of the currency that are equivalent to one US dollar.
A foreign currency has the property that the holder of the currency can earn interest at the risk-free interest rate prevailing in the foreign country. For example, the holder can invest the currency in a foreign-denominated bond. We define \\(r_{f}\\) as the value of the foreign risk-free interest rate when money is invested for time \\(T\\). The variable \\(r\\) is the risk-free rate when money is invested for this period of time in US dollars.\n\n
Table 5.4 shows currency futures quotes on May 14, 2013. The quotes are US dollars per unit of the foreign currency. (In the case of the Japanese yen, the quote is US dollars per 100 yen.) This is the usual quotation convention for futures contracts. Equation (5.9) applies with \\(r\\) equal to the US risk-free rate and \\(r_{f}\\) equal to the foreign risk-free rate.\n\nOn May 14, 2013, short-term interest rates on the Japanese yen, Swiss franc, and euro were lower than the short-term interest rate on the US dollar. This corresponds to the \\(r>r_{f}\\) situation and explains why futures prices for these currencies increase with maturity in Table 5.4. data.content:
Finance term: put–call parity,Futures option
Definition: The put-call parity relationship for European futures options can be derived through two distinct portfolios. 

**Portfolio A** consists of a European call futures option plus cash equal to \(Ke^{-rT}\). The call option can be exercised at maturity, resulting in the value of this portfolio at time \(T\) being:

\[
\max(F_{T},\ K)
\]

**Portfolio B** includes a European put futures option, a long futures contract, and cash equal to \(F_{0}e^{-rT}\) (where \(F_{0}\) is the futures price). At time \(T\), portfolio B's value is given by:

\[
F_{0} + (F_{T} - F_{0}) + \max(K - F_{T}, 0) = \max(F_{T},\ K)
\]

Since both portfolios exhibit equivalent value at time \(T\) and European options cannot be exercised early, their present values must also be equal. The value of portfolio A now is:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT}
\]

where \(c\) is the price of the call futures option. In contrast, due to daily settlement, portfolio B's current value is:

\[
p + F_{0}e^{-rT}
\]

where \(p\) pertains to the price of the put futures option. Thus, the put-call parity relationship is established as:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = p + F_{0}e^{-rT} \tag{18.1}
\]

In contrast to non-dividend-paying stock options, the stock price \(S_{0}\) is substituted by the discounted futures price \(F_{0}e^{-rT}\).

For American futures options, the relationship is represented as:

\[
F_{0}e^{-rT} - K < C - P < F_{0} - Ke^{-rT}
\]

The put-call parity relationship in equation (18.1) also delineates bounds for European call and put options. Given that the price of a put option \(p\) cannot be negative, it leads to:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} \geq F_{0}e^{-rT} 
\]

and thus,

\[
c \geq \max((F_{0} - K)e^{-rT}, 0)
\]

Conversely, since the price of a call option \(c\) cannot be negative, it follows:

\[
Ke^{-rT} \leq F_{0}e^{-rT} + p 
\]

resulting in:

\[
p \geq \max((K - F_{0})e^{-rT}, 0)
\]

These bounds are akin to those for European stock options. When options are deep in the money, the prices of European call and put options approach their lower bounds. For deep in-the-money call options, the associated put options become deep out of the money, causing \(p\) to approach zero, and consequently the difference between call price \(c\) and its lower bound mirrors \(p\). A similar logic applies to put options.

As American futures options can be exercised at any moment, it holds that:

\[
C \geq \max(F_{0} - K, 0) 
\]

and 

\[
C \geq \max(K - F_{0}, 0)
\]

Thus, assuming positive interest rates, the lower boundary for an American option price exceeds that of its corresponding European option price, as early exercise remains a potential advantage.

data.content:
Finance term: cash and,Short-term finance and planning
Definition: The article examines the components of cash and net working capital and their annual changes, essential for understanding short-term financing decisions. Current assets, which are assets expected to convert to cash within the year, include cash and cash equivalents, marketable securities, accounts receivable, and inventories. These current assets are listed on balance sheets based on their liquidity.

In contrast, current liabilities, representing obligations expected to require cash payment within the year, include accounts payable, expenses payable (such as accrued wages and taxes), and notes payable. 

Cash can be defined through the balance sheet identity:

\[
\text{Net working capital} + \text{Fixed assets} = \text{Long-term debt} + \text{Equity}
\]

where net working capital is calculated as:

\[
\text{Net working capital} = (\text{Cash} + \text{Other current assets}) - \text{Current liabilities}
\]

Substituting this into the balance sheet identity gives:

\[
\text{Cash} = \text{Long-term debt} + \text{Equity} + \text{Current liabilities} - \text{Current assets other than cash} - \text{Fixed assets}
\]

This formulation indicates activities that can either increase or decrease cash. The following lists categorize these activities:

**ACTIVITIES THAT INCREASE CASH:**
- Increasing long-term debt (borrowing over the long term)
- Increasing equity (selling some stock)
- Increasing current liabilities (getting a 90-day loan)
- Decreasing current assets other than cash (selling some inventory for cash)
- Decreasing fixed assets (selling some property)

**ACTIVITIES THAT DECREASE CASH:**
- Decreasing long-term debt (paying off a long-term debt)
- Decreasing equity (repurchasing some stock)
- Decreasing current liabilities (paying off a 90-day loan)
- Increasing current assets other than cash (buying some inventory for cash)
- Increasing fixed assets (buying some property)

These two categories reflect opposite actions; for instance, floating a long-term bond increases cash, while paying it off decreases cash. 

Activities that increase cash are referred to as sources of cash, defined as actions that raise liabilities (or equity) or liquidate assets, resulting in cash inflows. Conversely, uses of cash involve the reduction of liabilities or acquisition of assets, necessitating cash outflows.

Finance term: change in net working capital,Cash flow
Definition: In addition to investing in fixed assets, a firm will also invest in current assets. For example, going back to the balance sheets in Table 2.1, we see that at the end of 2007, U.S. had current assets of $1,403. At the end of 2006, current assets were $1,112; so, during the year, U.S. invested $1,403 - 1,112 = $291 in current assets.\n\nAs the firm changes its investment in current assets, its current liabilities will usually change as well. To determine the change in net working capital, the easiest approach is just to take the difference between the beginning and ending net working capital (WWC) figures. Net working capital at the end of 2007 was $1,403 - 389 = $1,014. Similarly, at the end of 2006, net working capital was $1,112 - 428 = $684. Given these figures, we have the following:n\nNet working capital thus increased by $330. Put another way, U.S. Corporation had a net investment of $330 in NWC for the year. This change in NWC is often referred to as the \"addition to\" NWC.

\hline

\hline

data.content:
Finance term: annual percentage rate and,Effective annual rate (EAR)
Definition: The **annual percentage rate (APR)** is a required disclosure on nearly all consumer loans in the United States, mandated by truth-in-lending laws. However, it is often confused with the effective annual rate (EAR). When a bank quotes a car loan at 12 percent APR, it does not mean the consumer is actually paying 12 percent interest. The APR is calculated as the interest rate per period multiplied by the number of periods in a year. For instance, if a bank charges 1.2 percent per month, the APR is 1.2% × 12 = 14.4%. Therefore, an APR of 12 percent corresponds to a monthly interest rate of 1 percent. The calculation for EAR in this scenario is:

\[
\text{EAR} = [1 + (\text{APR}/12)]^{12} - 1 = 1.01^{12} - 1 = 12.6825\%
\]

Despite being called an annual rate, the APR can mislead consumers about the actual cost of borrowing. Moreover, truth-in-saving laws require institutions to disclose an "annual percentage yield" (APY) for savings accounts, which is in fact an EAR. This discrepancy means that borrowers (APRs) and savers (APYs) are not provided the same type of rate.

A significant difference arises between APR and EAR, particularly with high-interest loans like **payday loans**. These short-term loans typically last less than two weeks. In an example from AmeriCash Advance, a consumer writes a postdated check for $125, receiving $100 immediately. The interest rate for 15 days can be calculated using the future value (FV) equation:

\[
\text{FV} = \text{PV} \times (1 + r)^{\text{t}}
\]

Substituting in the known values:

\[
125 = 100 \times (1 + r)^{1} \implies 1.25 = (1 + r) \implies r = 0.25 \text{ or } 25\%
\]

This 25% is the interest for just 15 days. The APR becomes:

\[
\text{APR} = .25 \times (365/15) = 6.08333 \text{ or } 608.33\%
\]

The EAR for this payday loan can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{EAR} = (1 + \text{Quoted rate}/m)^{\text{w}} - 1 = (1 + .25)^{w/3} - 1 \implies \text{EAR} = 227.1096 \text{ or } 22,710.96\%
\]

National Payday allows a similar loan but extends the repayment period to 18 days. The APR for this arrangement is calculated to be 506.94 percent, leading to an EAR of 9,128.26 percent.

In summary, consumers should exercise caution when interpreting APR and EAR, especially concerning high-interest loans, as the actual costs can be significantly higher than what APR figures suggest.

The initial margin is $2,000 per contract, and the maintenance margin is $1,500 per contract. The company's policy is to hedge 80% of its exposure. Contracts with maturities up to 13 months into the future are considered to have sufficient liquidity to meet the company’s needs.What is the future price paid for copper in February 2015 per pound? (Unit: cent)

data.content:
Finance term: Stack and roll
Definition: The process of managing hedge expiration dates involves rolling forward futures contracts when the hedge expiration surpasses the delivery dates of available futures. This strategy is referred to as _stack and roll_. For example, a company employing a short hedge to mitigate the risk of selling an asset at time \(T\) can utilize several futures contracts with progressively later delivery dates.

The rolling procedure involves the following steps: 
- At time \(t_1\), short the first futures contract.
- At time \(t_2\), close out the first contract and short the second.
- This process continues until the final contract at time \(T\) is closed out.

Consider a situation where a company realizes it will have 100,000 barrels of oil to sell in June 2015 and decides to hedge with a ratio of 1.0. The current spot price is $89. Assuming only the first six delivery months have sufficient liquidity, the company shorts 100 October 2014 contracts. 

As time progresses:
- In September 2014, the hedge is rolled forward into the March 2015 contract.
- In February 2015, it is rolled forward again into the July 2015 contract.

In this example, the following outcomes occur:
- The October 2014 contract is shorted at $88.20 per barrel and closed out at $87.40, resulting in a profit of $0.80 per barrel.
- The March 2015 contract is shorted at $87.00 and closed at $86.50, yielding a profit of $0.50.
- The July 2015 contract is shorted at $86.30 and closed at $85.90, for a profit of $0.40.

The total dollar gain per barrel from the short futures contracts is calculated as follows:

\[
(88.20-87.40) + (87.00-86.50) + (86.30-85.90) = 1.70
\]

Despite this hedging strategy, oil prices drop from $89 to $86, resulting in only $1.70 per barrel compensation for a $3.00 decline in price. This outcome highlights that total compensation for a decline is not always realized when futures prices are below spot prices; the goal is to lock in a reasonable futures price corresponding to June 2015 if actively traded.

In practical scenarios, companies generally face ongoing exposure to their underlying asset and use 1-month futures contracts due to their liquidity. They initially stack contracts to cover their exposure until the end of the hedging horizon. After one month, they close all contracts and roll them into new 1-month contracts to address their evolving exposure.

A notable case is that of Metallgesellschaft, a German company in the early 1990s, which faced difficulties using this strategy. As the prices of commodities fell, it incurred immediate cash outflows from futures while awaiting gains from contracts, leading to liquidity issues due to mismatched cash flows between hedge timing and the asset position being hedged. Such potential liquidity problems must be carefully considered when planning a hedging strategy.

Finance term: Constant growth model
Definition: Suppose we know that the dividend for some company always grows at a steady rate. Call this growth rate g. If we let D_0 be the dividend just paid, then the next dividend, D_1, is:
D_1 = D_0 \times (1 + g)
As long as the growth rate, g, is less than the discount rate, R, the present value of this series of cash flows can be written simply as:
P_{0} = \frac{D_{0} \times (1 + g)}{R - g} = \frac{D_{1}}{R - g}

Finance term: scenario analysis,What-if analyses
Definition: What-if analysis involves scenario analysis, which examines changes in NPV estimates based on different projections, such as adjusting unit sales from 6,000 to 5,500. By exploring various scenarios, we may find that many plausible cases yield positive NPVs, providing confidence in proceeding with a project. Conversely, if a significant percentage displays negative NPVs, the forecasting risk is high, warranting further investigation.

The analysis begins with the worst-case scenario, determining the minimum NPV. If this remains positive, the project's viability improves. In this scenario, unfavorable values are assigned, including low units sold and prices, along with high costs. Conversely, the best case considers favorable conditions, setting an upper bound on NPV. For example, in the worst-case scenario, the cash flow is positive at $24,490, but the return is -14.4%, leading to an NPV of -$111,719. Given a project cost of $200,000, this could result in losing over half of the original investment. In contrast, the best case offers a 41% return.

Terms like "best case" and "worst case" might be misleading. Instead, the terms "optimistic" and "pessimistic" are more accurate. The best case reflects high-end assumptions of reasonable projections, while the worst case corresponds to low-end figures.

Specific scenarios vary widely. For instance, Ivannabe Mines assessed a copper and gold mine, using base metal prices of $400 per ounce for gold and $0.90 per ounce for copper, with a report claiming accuracy within ±35%. This range can establish best-case and worst-case scenarios.

A minimum analysis includes two intermediate cases, yielding five total scenarios (best case, worst case, base case, and two intermediate cases). However, excessive analysis can lead to "paralysis of analysis," where generating too many possibilities results in uncertainty regarding decision-making. Scenario analysis is beneficial for understanding potential outcomes and assessing disaster risks but does not dictate whether a project should be undertaken.

Real-world cases often demonstrate that worst-case scenarios can fall short. For instance, the Channel Tunnel, a significant construction project, ultimately cost $17.9 billion—over twice the initial estimate of $8.8 billion. Moreover, it attracted only 4 million passengers in its first year, far below forecasts of 16.8 million, leading to revenue significantly under projections; actual revenue for 2003 was only about one-third of the expected $2.88 billion. This miscalculation stemmed from increased competition from ferry services and low-cost airlines.

Similarly, the Segway, envisioned as an alternative to cars, faced setbacks when it recalled its transporters for a software upgrade and saw only 16,000 sales instead of the projected 50,000 to 100,000 units in its first five months. 

Considering the unpredictable nature of outcomes and external factors, traditional best-case and worst-case scenarios may not suffice in accurately assessing a project's feasibility.

Finance term: residual dividend approach,establishing a,Dividend policy
Definition: Firms with higher dividend payouts often need to sell stock more frequently, which can be expensive. To minimize the need for new equity sales and maintain their capital structure, firms can rely on internally generated equity to finance positive NPV projects. Dividends can only be paid out of leftover earnings, termed as the _residual_. Such a dividend policy is known as a **residual dividend approach**.

Under this policy, a firm prioritizes its investment needs and maintains a desired debt-equity ratio before paying dividends. For example, if a firm has $1,000 in earnings and a debt-equity ratio of 0.50, it has 50 cents of debt for every $1.50 in total value. To determine the funds available without selling new equity, if the firm reinvests all $1,000, equity increases by $1,000 and an additional $500 must be borrowed, totaling $1,500.

The decision to pay dividends hinges on comparing available funds ($1,500) with planned capital spending. If spending exceeds available funds, dividends are not paid, and new equity may need to be raised or capital projects postponed. Conversely, if available funds exceed spending, the remaining earnings constitute the dividend.

For example, with $900 in planned capital spending, to maintain a debt-equity ratio of 0.50, the firm finances $300 through debt and $600 through internal funds. This results in a $400 residual dividend ($1,000 - $600). Consequently, aftertax earnings are $1,000, dividends are $400, retained earnings are $600, and new borrowing totals $300, maintaining the debt-equity ratio at 0.50.

The relationship between physical investment and dividend payout can be summarized through various scenarios. In Row 1, with a new investment of $3,000, the additional debt needed is $1,000, while equity contribution totals $2,000 to maintain the debt-equity ratio. Given that the equity needed exceeds earnings, all earnings are retained, leading to no dividend payout.

Rows 2 and 3 exhibit decreased investments and a corresponding drop in additional debt needed, but since equity requirements remain above $1,000, dividends again are not paid. 

Row 4 presents a scenario with an investment of $1,000, where $333 is financed through debt. The remaining $667 comes from internal funds, resulting in a $333 residual for dividends. No new stock is issued here.

In Rows 5 and 6, as investments decrease further, new debt requirements and retained earnings also reduce, allowing for an increase in dividends, while avoiding stock issuance. 

The observed trend is that firms with more investment opportunities tend to have lower dividend payout ratios, whereas those with fewer opportunities tend to distribute a higher percentage of earnings as dividends. This pattern reflects in the real world where young, fast-growing firms have low payout ratios, while older, slower-growing firms usually exhibit higher ratios.

\centering
\caption{Example of Dividend Policy under the Residual Approach}
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Row} & \textbf{Aftertax Earnings} & \textbf{New Investment} & \textbf{Additional Debt} & \textbf{Retained Earnings} & \textbf{Additional Stock} & \textbf{Dividends} \\ \hline
1 & \$1,000 & \$3,000 & \$1,000 & \$1,000 & \$1,000 & \$0 \\ \hline
2 & 1,000 & 2,000 & 667 & 1,000 & 333 & 0 \\ \hline
3 & 1,000 & 1,500 & 500 & 1,000 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline
4 & 1,000 & 1,000 & 333 & 667 & 0 & 333 \\ \hline
5 & 1,000 & 500 & 167 & 333 & 0 & 667 \\ \hline
6 & 1,000 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1,000 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

data.content:
Finance term: basic approach,weighted average cost of capital and,Flotation costs
Definition: We start with a simple case. The Spatt Company, an all-equity firm, has a cost of equity of 20 percent. Because this firm is 100 percent equity, its WACC and its cost of equity are the same. Spatt is contemplating a large-scale $100 million expansion of its existing opera- tions. The expansion would be funded by selling new stock. 

 Based on conversations with its investment banker, Spatt believes its flotation costs will run 10 percent of the amount issued. This means that Spatt’s proceeds from the equity sale will be only 90 percent of the amount sold. When flotation costs are considered, what is the cost of the expansion? 

 As we discuss in more detail in Chapter 16, Spatt needs to sell enough equity to raise $100 million after covering the flotation costs. In other words: 
 $100 million = (1 - .10) 	imes Amount raised 
 Amount raised = $100 million/.90 = $111.11 million 

 Spatt’s flotation costs are thus $11.11 million, and the true cost of the expansion is $111.11 million once we include flotation costs. 

 Things are only slightly more complicated if the firm uses both debt and equity. For example, suppose Spatt’s target capital structure is 60 percent equity, 40 percent debt. The flotation costs associated with equity are still 10 percent, but the flotation costs for debt are less—say 5 percent. 

 Earlier, when we had different capital costs for debt and equity, we calculated a weighted average cost of capital using the target capital structure weights. Here we will do much the same thing. We can calculate a weighted average flotation cost, f_A, by multiplying the equity flotation cost, f_E, by the percentage of equity (E/V) and the debt flotation cost, fD, by the percentage of debt (D/V) and then adding the two together: 
 f_A=(E/V)	imes f_E + (D/V) 	imes f_D = 60% 	imes .10 + 40% 	imes .05 

 The weighted average flotation cost is thus 8 percent. What this tells us is that for every dollar in outside financing needed for new projects, the firm must actually raise $1!(1 $ .08) ! $1.087. In our example, the project cost is $100 million when we ignore flotation costs. If we include them, then the true cost is $100 million!(1 $ fA) ! $100 million!.92 ! $108.7 million. 

 In taking issue costs into account, the firm must be careful not to use the wrong weights. The firm should use the target weights, even if it can finance the entire cost of the project with either debt or equity. The fact that a firm can finance a specific project with debt or equity is not directly relevant. If a firm has a target debt-equity ratio of 1, for example, but chooses to finance a particular project with all debt, it will have to raise additional equity later on to maintain its target debt-equity ratio. To take this into account, the firm should always use the target weights in calculating the flotation cost.

Finance term: carrying costs and,Economic order quantity (EOQ) model
Definition: As Figure 2.3 illustrates, carrying costs are normally assumed to be directly proportional to inventory levels. Suppose we let \(Q\) be the quantity of inventory that Eyssell orders each time (3,600 units); we will call this the _restocking quantity_. Average inventory would then just be \(Q/2\), or 1,800 units. If we let CC be the carrying cost per unit per year, Eyssell's total carrying costs will be:

\[\begin{split}\text{Total carrying costs}&=\text{ Average inventory}\times\text{Carrying costs per unit}\\ &=(Q/2)\times\text{CC}\end{split}\]

In Eyssell's case, if carrying costs were $.75 per unit per year, total carrying costs would be the average inventory of 1,800 multiplied by $.75, or $1,350 per year.

question: Suppose the money supply M has been growing at 10% per year and nominal GDP YP has been growing at 20% per year.What is the velocity in 2012?
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Velocity of Money and Equation of Exchange,Quantity Theory of Money
Definition: The clearest exposition of the classical quantity theory approach is found in the work of the American economist Irving Fisher, in his influential book _The Purchasing Power of Money_, published in 1911. Fisher wanted to examine the link between the total quantity of money \\(M\\) (the money supply) and the total amount of spending on final goods and services produced in the economy P \times Y, where P is the price level and Y is aggregate output (income). (Total spending P \times Y is also thought of as aggregate nominal income for the economy or as nominal GDP) The concept that provides the link between M and P \times Y is called the **velocity of money** (often reduced to velocity), the average number of times per year (turnover) that a dollar is spent in buying the total amount of goods and services produced in the economy. Velocity V is defined more precisely as total spending P \times Y divided by the quantity of money _M_:
V = \frac{P \times Y}{M}
If, for example, nominal GDP (P \times Y) in a year is $5 trillion and the quantity of money is $1 trillion, velocity is 5, meaning that the average dollar bill is spent five times in purchasing final goods and services in the economy.
By multiplying both sides of this definition by M, we obtain the **equation of exchange**, which relates nominal income to the quantity of money and velocity:
M \times V = P \times Y
The equation of exchange thus states that the quantity of money multiplied by the number of times that this money is spent in a given year must equal nominal income (the total nominal amount spent on goods and services in that year).
As it stands, this equation is nothing more than an identity—a relationship that is true by definition. It does not tell us, for instance, that when the money supply M changes, nominal income (P \times Y) changes in the same direction; a rise in M, for example, could be offset by a fall in V that leaves M \times V (and therefore P \times Y) unchanged. To convert het equation of exchange (an identity) into a theory of how nominal income is determined requires an understanding of the factors that determine velocity.
Irving Fisher reasoned that velocity is determined by the institutions in an economy that affect the way individuals conduct transactions. If people use charge accounts and credit cards to conduct their transactions, as they can today, and consequently use  money less often when making purchases, less money is required to conduct the transactions generated by nominal income (M falls relative to P \times Y), and velocity (P \times Y)/M will increase. Conversely, if it is more convenient for purchases to be paid for with cash or checks (both of which are money), more money is used to conduct the transactions generated by the same level of nominal income, and velocity will fall. Fisher took the view that the institutional and technological features of the economy would affect velocity only slowly over time, so velocity would normally be reasonably constant in the short run.

data.content:
Finance term: T-account,Basic Banking
Definition: A T-account is a simplified balance sheet that tracks the changes in balance sheet items starting from an initial position. For example, when Jane Brown opens a checking account with a $100 bill, she has a $100 checkable deposit at First National Bank, which appears as a $100 liability on the bank's balance sheet. The bank then stores her $100 bill as vault cash, increasing its assets by $100. The T-account for First National Bank is as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\multicolumn{4}{l}{First National Bank} \\
\multicolumn{2}{l}{Assets} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Liabilities} \\
Vault cash & +\$100 & Checkable deposits & +\$100  
\end{array}
\]

Since vault cash is also part of the bank's reserves, the T-account can be rewritten as:

\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\multicolumn{2}{l}{Assets} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Liabilities} \\
Reserves & +\$100 & Checkable deposits & +\$100  
\end{array}
\]

When Jane opens her account with a $100 check from another bank, such as Second National Bank, the T-account for First National Bank shows:

\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\multicolumn{2}{l}{Assets} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Liabilities} \\
Cash items in process of collection & +\$100 & Checkable deposits & +\$100  
\end{array}
\]

In this case, checkable deposits increase by $100, but the First National Bank is owed $100 by Second National Bank, recorded as cash items in process of collection. To collect these funds, First National Bank deposits the check in its account at the Federal Reserve (Fed), which subsequently transfers $100 of reserves from Second National Bank to First National Bank. The final balance sheet for both banks looks like this:

First National Bank:

\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\multicolumn{4}{l}{First National Bank} \\
\multicolumn{2}{l}{Assets} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Liabilities} \\
Reserves & +\$100 & Checkable deposits & +\$100  
\end{array}
\]

Second National Bank:

\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\multicolumn{4}{l}{Second National Bank} \\
\multicolumn{2}{l}{Assets} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Liabilities} \\
Reserves & -\$100 & Checkable deposits & -\$100  
\end{array}
\]

This illustrates that when a check written on an account at one bank is deposited in another bank, the receiving bank gains reserves equal to the check amount, while the bank that issued the check sees its reserves decrease by the same amount. Consequently, when a bank receives additional deposits, it gains an equal amount of reserves, and when it loses deposits, it loses an equal amount of reserves.

data.content:
Finance term: values,Bonds
Definition: Just like any financial instrument, bonds are affected by fluctuations in interest rates. As marketplace interest rates change, the cash flows from a bond remain constant, leading to variations in the bond's market value. When interest rates rise, the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows declines, reducing its value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, the bond's value increases.

To accurately assess the value of a bond at any given time, it is crucial to know the following: the number of periods remaining until maturity, the bond's face value, the coupon payments, and the prevailing market interest rate for similar bonds. This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

Finance term: sustainable rate of,growth and,External financing needed (EFN)
Definition: We have seen that if the Hoffman Company wishes to grow more rapidly than at a rate of 9.65 percent per year, external financing must be arranged. The second growth rate of interest is the maximum growth rate a firm can achieve with no external _equity_ financing while it maintains a constant debt-equity ratio. This rate is commonly called the **sustainable growth rate** because it is the maximum rate of growth a firm can maintain without increasing its financial leverage.

There are various reasons why a firm might wish to avoid equity sales. For example, as we discuss in Chapter 16, new equity sales can be expensive. Alternatively, the current owners may not wish to bring in new owners or contribute additional equity. Why a firm might view a particular debt-equity ratio as optimal is discussed in Chapters 15 and 17; for now, we will take it as given.

Based on Table 4.8, the sustainable growth rate for Hoffman is approximately 20 percent because the debt-equity ratio is near 1.0 at that growth rate. The precise value can be calculated (see Problem 32 at the end of the chapter):

\[\text{Sustainable growth rate}=\frac{\text{ROE}\times b}{1-\text{ROE}\times b}\]

This is identical to the internal growth rate except that ROE, return on equity, is used instead of ROA.

data.content:
Finance term: futures option,Binomial tree
Definition: The article addresses the valuation of futures options using binomial models. It begins with a futures price \(F_0\) that can increase to \(F_0 u\) or decrease to \(F_0 d\) over time \(T\). The option's payoff is represented as \(f_u\) if the price increases and \(f_d\) if it decreases. The riskless portfolio consists of a short position in one option and a long position in \(\Delta\) futures contracts, defined by:

\[
\Delta = \frac{f_u - f_d}{F_0 u - F_0 d}
\]

At time \(T\), the value of the portfolio is:

\[
(F_0 u - F_0) \Delta - f_u
\]

To find the present value of this portfolio, the risk-free interest rate \(r\) is considered, leading to the formula:

\[
\text{Value today} = [(F_0 u - F_0) \Delta - f_u] e^{-rT}
\]

The present value can also be expressed as \(-f\), with \(f\) being the current value of the option, resulting in:

\[
-f = [(F_0 u - F_0) \Delta - f_u] e^{-rT}
\]

Substituting for \(\Delta\) and simplifying yields:

\[
f = e^{-rT} [p f_u + (1 - p) f_d] \tag{18.5}
\]

where \(p\) represents the risk-neutral probability of an up movement:

\[
p = \frac{1 - d}{u - d} \tag{18.6}
\]

In the provided numerical example, specific values are given: \(u = 1.1\), \(d = 0.9333\), \(r = 0.06\), \(T = \frac{1}{12}\), \(f_u = 4\), and \(f_d = 0\). Using equation (18.6), the risk-neutral probability \(p\) is calculated as:

\[
p = \frac{1 - 0.9333}{1.1 - 0.9333} = 0.4
\]

The riskless portfolio consists of a short position in one option and a long position in \(\Delta\) futures contracts, defined by:

\[
\Delta = \frac{f_u - f_d}{F_0 u - F_0 d}
\]

At time \(T\), the value of the portfolio is:

\[
(F_0 u - F_0) \Delta - f_u
\]

To find the present value of this portfolio, the risk-free interest rate \(r\) is considered, leading to the formula:

\[
\text{Value today} = [(F_0 u - F_0) \Delta - f_u] e^{-rT}
\]

question: Jude Corp. has 9 percent coupon bonds making annual payments with a YTM of 6.3 percent. The current yield on these bonds is 7.1 percent.How many years do these bonds have left until they mature?
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: values,Bonds
Definition: Just like any financial instrument, bonds are affected by fluctuations in interest rates. As marketplace interest rates change, the cash flows from a bond remain constant, leading to variations in the bond's market value. When interest rates rise, the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows declines, reducing its value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, the bond's value increases.

To accurately assess the value of a bond at any given time, it is crucial to know the following: the number of periods remaining until maturity, the bond's face value, the coupon payments, and the prevailing market interest rate for similar bonds. This required market interest rate is referred to as the bond's **yield to maturity (YTM)**, often abbreviated to the bond's _yield_. Using this information, the present value of the cash flows from the bond can be calculated to estimate its current market value.

For example, consider a bond issued by Xarth Co. with 10 years to maturity, an annual coupon of $80, and a prevailing yield to maturity of 8 percent. The bond will make annual coupon payments of $80 for the next 10 years, plus a payment of $1,000 at maturity. The cash flows can be categorized into an annuity (the coupon payments) and a lump sum (the face value). 

The present value of the $1,000 payment in 10 years at an 8 percent yield can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.08^{10}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.1589} = \$463.19
\]

Next, to find the present value of the annuity stream from the coupons:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.08^{10}})}{0.08} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.1589})}{0.08} = \$80 \times 6.7101 = \$536.81
\]

Adding these values together provides the bond's total value:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$463.19 + 536.81 = \$1,000
\]

This bond sells for its face value because the market interest rate matches the coupon rate at 8 percent.

If one year passes and the market interest rate rises to 10 percent, the bond now has nine years until maturity. The calculations for the bond's value must be updated accordingly. The present value of the $1,000 payment due in nine years at a 10 percent yield is:

\[
\text{Present value} = \frac{\$1,000}{1.10^{9}} = \frac{\$1,000}{2.3579} = \$424.10
\]

For the annual coupon payments over nine years at the new yield:

\[
\text{Annuity present value} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{1.10^{9}})}{0.10} = \$80 \times \frac{(1 - \frac{1}{2.3579})}{0.10} = \$80 \times 5.7590 = \$460.72
\]

Thus, the updated total bond value is:

\[
\text{Total bond value} = \$424.10 + 460.72 = \$884.82
\]

Therefore, the bond is now valued at approximately $885, indicating that it is priced to yield 10 percent at this new market value.

In general, the value of a bond can be expressed as follows:

\[
\text{Bond value} = C \times \frac{[1-1/(1+r)^{t}]}{r} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^{t}}
\]

This formula encapsulates the present value of both the coupons and the face amount paid at maturity.

Definition: The Trans Am Corporation currently has no debt in its capital structure. The CFO, Ms. Morris, is considering a restructuring that would involve issuing debt and using the proceeds to buy back some of the outstanding equity. Table 7.3 presents both the current and proposed capital structures. As shown, the firm's assets have a market value of $8 million, and there are 400,000 shares outstanding. Because Trans Am is an all-equid risk firm, the price per share is $20.\n\nThe proposed debt issue would raise $4 million; the interest rate would be 10 percent. Because the stock sells for $20 per share, the $4 million in new debt would be used to purchase $4 million/2 = 200,000 shares, leaving 200,000. After the restructuring, Trans Am would have a capital structure that was 50 percent debt, so the debt-equity ratio would be 1. Notice that, for now, we assume that the stock price will remain at $20.\n\nTo investigate the impact of the proposed restructuring, Ms. Morris has prepared Table 7.4, which compares the firm's current capital structure to the proposed capital structure under three scenarios. The scenarios reflect different assumptions about the firm's EBIT. Under the expected scenario, the EBIT is $1 million. In the recession scenario, EBIT falls to $500,000. In the expansion scenario, it rises to $1.5 million.\n\nTo illustrate some of the calculations behind the figures in Table 7.4, consider the expansion case. EBIT is $1.5 million. With no debt (the current capital structure) and no taxes, net income is also $1.5 million. In this case, there are 400,000 shares worth $8 million total. EPS is therefore $1.5 million/400,000 = $3.75. Also, because accounting return on equity, ROE, is net income divided by total equity, ROE is $1.5 million/8 million = 18.75%. \n\n With S4 million in debt (the proposed capital structure), things are somewhat different. Because the interest rate is 10 percent, the interest bill is $400,000. With EBIT of $1.5 million, interest of $400,000, and no taxes, net income is $1.1 million. Now there are only 200,000 shares worth $4 million total. EPS is therefore $1.1 million/200,000 = $5.50, versus the $3.75 that we calculated in the previous scenario. Finance term: implementing the approach,cost of equity and,Security market line (SML)
Definition: In Chapter 13, we discussed the security market line, or SML. Our primary conclusion was that the required or expected return on a risky investment depends on three things:

1. The risk-free rate, \(R_{f}\).
2. The market risk premium, E(\(R_{u}\)) - \(R_{f}\).
3. The systematic risk of the asset relative to average, which we called its beta coefficient, b.

Using the SML, we can write the expected return on the company's equity, E(\(R_{b}\)), as:

\[\text{E}(R_{\text{g}}) = R_{\text{f}} + \text{b}_{\text{g}} \times \left[ \text{E}(R_{\text{g}u}) - R_{\text{f}} \right\rbrack\]

where bg is the estimated beta. To make the SML approach consistent with the dividend growth model, we will drop the _E_s denoting expectations and henceforth write the required return from the SML, \(R_{c}\), as:

\[R_{\text{g}} = R_{\text{f}} + \text{b}_{\text{g}} \times (R_{M} - R_{\text{f}} )\] 
 Implementing the ApproachTo use the SML approach, we need a risk-free rate, \(R_{t}\), an estimate of the market risk premium, \(R_{M}-R_{f}\), and an estimate of the relevant beta, \(\beta_{x}\). In Chapter 12 (Table 12.3), we saw that one estimate of the market risk premium (based on large common stocks) is 8.5 percent. U.S. Treasury bills are paying about 4.9 percent as this chapter is being written, so we will use this as our risk-free rate. Beta coefficients for publicly traded companies are widely available. 
 To illustrate, in Chapter 13, we saw that eBay had an estimated beta of 1.35 (Table 13.8). We could thus estimate eBay’s cost of equity as: 
 
R_{eBay} = R_f +  eta_{eBay} 	imes (R_M - R_f) = 4.9% + 1.35 	imes 8.5% = 16.38% 
 Thus, using the SML approach, we calculate that eBay’s cost of equity is about 16.38 percent.

Finance term: Homemade leverage
Definition: Based on Tables 17.3 and 17.4 and Figure 17.1, Ms. Morris draws the following conclusions:\n\n1. The effect of financial leverage depends on the company's EBIT. When EBIT is relatively high, leverage is beneficial.\n2. Under the expected scenario, leverage increases the returns to shareholders, as measured by both ROE and EPS.\n\n 3. Shareholders are exposed to more risk under the proposed capital structure because the EPS and ROE are much more sensitive to changes in EBIT in this case.\n4. Because of the impact that financial leverage has on both the expected return to stockholders and the riskiness of the stock, capital structure is an important consideration.\n\nThe first three of these conclusions are clearly correct. Does the last conclusion necessarily follow? Surprisingly, the answer is no. As we discuss next, the reason is that shareholders can adjust the amount of financial leverage by borrowing and lending on their own. This use of personal borrowing to alter the degree of financial leverage is called **homemade leverage**.\n\nWe will now illustrate that it actually makes no difference whether or not Trans Am adopts the proposed capital structure, because any stockholder who prefers the proposed capital structure can simply create it using homemade leverage. To begin, the first part of Table 17.5 shows what will happen to an investor who buys $2,000 worth of Trans Am stock if the proposed capital structure is adopted. This investor purchases 100 shares of stock. From Table 17.4, we know that EPS will be $.50, $3, or $5.50, so the total earnings for 100 shares will be either $50, $300, or $550 under the proposed capital structure.\n\nNow, suppose that Trans Am does not adopt the proposed capital structure. In this case, EPS will be $1.25, $2.50, or $3.75. The second part of Table 17.5 demonstrates how a stockholder who prefers the payoffs under the proposed structure can create them using personal borrowing. To do this, the stockholder borrows $2,000 at 10 percent on her or his own. Our investor uses this amount, along with the original $2,000, to buy 200 shares of stock. As shown, the net payoffs are exactly the same as those for the proposed capital structure.\n\nHow did we know to borrow $2,000 to create the right payoffs? We are trying to replicate Trans Am's proposed capital structure at the personal level. The proposed capital structure results in a debt-equity ratio of 1. To replicate this structure at the personal level, the stockholder must borrow enough to create this same debt-equity ratio. Because the stockholder has $2,000 in equity invested, the borrowing of another $2,000 will create a personal debt-equity ratio of 1.\n\nThis example demonstrates that investors can always increase financial leverage themselves to create a different pattern of payoffs. It thus makes no difference whether Trans Am chooses the proposed capital structure.

    \centering
    \caption{Proposed Capital Structure versus Original Capital Structure with Homemade Leverage}
    \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
        \hline
        \textbf{Proposed Capital Structure} & \textbf{Recession} & \textbf{Expected} & \textbf{Expansion} \\ \hline
        EPS & \$ .50 & \$ 3.00 & \$ 5.50 \\ \hline
        Earnings for 100 shares & 50.00 & 300.00 & 550.00 \\ \hline
        Net cost & 100 shares $\times$ \$20 = \$2,000 &  &  \\ \hline
         &  &  & \\ 
        \textbf{Original Capital Structure and Homemade Leverage} &  &  &  \\ \hline
        EPS & \$ 1.25 & \$ 2.50 & \$ 3.75 \\ \hline
        Earnings for 200 shares & 250.00 & 500.00 & 750.00 \\ \hline
        Less: Interest on \$2,000 at 10\% & 200.00 & 200.00 & 200.00 \\ \hline
        Net earnings & \$ 50.00 & \$ 300.00 & \$ 550.00 \\ \hline
        Net cost & 200 shares $\times$ \$20 - Amount borrowed = \$4,000 - 2,000 = \$2,000 &  &  \\ \hline
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Finance term: foreign currency options,Black–Scholes–Merton and volatility smile
Definition: The volatility smile is a crucial concept in pricing foreign currency options, characterized by lower implied volatility for at-the-money options and higher volatility for options moving into or out of the money. The volatility smile depicted in Figure 20.1 relates to the implied distribution shown in Figure 20.2, which reveals that the implied distribution has heavier tails compared to a lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation. This phenomenon is referred to as _kurtosis_, which indicates that both extreme small and large movements in exchange rates are more likely under the implied distribution than under the lognormal distribution, while intermediate movements are less probable.

To analyze the relationship between the volatility smile and the implied distribution, consider a deep-out-of-the-money call option with a strike price of \( K_{2} \). This option will only pay off if the exchange rate exceeds \( K_{2} \). The implied probability distribution in Figure 20.2 shows a higher likelihood of this event compared to a lognormal distribution, suggesting a higher price and therefore a higher implied volatility for the option as seen in Figure 20.1. A similar logic applies to deep-out-of-the-money put options with a low strike price of \( K_{1} \), where the probability that the exchange rate falls below \( K_{1} \) is also higher under the implied distribution, leading again to a higher option price and implied volatility.

Exchange rates deviate from lognormal distribution for two main reasons: constant volatility and smooth price changes with no jumps are not present in practical scenarios. Exchange rates exhibit nonconstant volatility and frequent jumps, which enhance the likelihood of extreme outcomes. 

The effects of nonconstant volatility and jumps on option pricing vary with the option's maturity. For longer maturities, the impact of nonconstant volatility on prices becomes more significant; conversely, its effect on implied volatility tends to diminish. As the maturity of the option increases, the influence of jumps on both prices and implied volatility also decreases. Consequently, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced with longer option maturities. This behavior underscores the complexities underlying foreign currency options pricing and the inherent risks associated with exchange rate fluctuations.

data.content:
Finance term: with multiple cash flows,Present value (PV)
Definition: Determining the present value of future cash flows can be approached in two primary ways: discounting each cash flow one period at a time or calculating each present value individually and summing them.

For example, to find out how much money to invest today to obtain $1,000 in one year and $2,000 in two years at a 9% return, we calculate the present value of each cash flow:

1. The present value of $2,000 in two years at 9%:
   \[
   \text{PV} = \frac{\text{$2,000}}{1.09^{2}} = \text{$1,683.36}
   \]

2. The present value of $1,000 in one year:
   \[
   \text{PV} = \frac{\text{$1,000}}{1.09} = \text{$917.43}
   \]

Adding these amounts gives the total present value:
\[
\text{Total PV} = \text{$1,683.36} + \text{$917.43} = \text{$2,600.79}
\]

To verify this amount, if $2,600.79 is invested today at 9%, the future values can be calculated as follows: after one year, it grows to:
\[
\text{$2,600.79} \times 1.09 = \text{$2,834.86}
\]
Subtracting the $1,000 needed after one year leaves:
\[
\text{$2,834.86} - \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,834.86}
\]
In the second year, this amount further accrues interest:
\[
\text{$1,834.86} \times 1.09 = \text{$2,000}
\]
This checks out according to the planned future cash flows.

An alternative method of calculating present values for recurring cash flows, such as receiving $1,000 at the end of each year for five years, involves discounting each cash flow separately and summing them. For instance, at a 6% discount rate, the present value is calculated as:
\[
\text{PV} = \sum \frac{\text{$1,000}}{(1.06)^t} \quad (t = 1 \text{ to } 5)
\]

In another approach, you can recursively discount cash flows back to the present. For example, starting with the last cash flow:
\[
\text{PV} = \frac{\text{$1,000}}{1.06} + 1,000 = \text{$943.40} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,943.40}
\]
This discounted amount can then be added to the cash flow from the next year, giving:
\[
\frac{\text{$1,943.40}}{1.06} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$1,833.40} + \text{$1,000} = \text{$2,833.40}
\]

This process of discounting and summing can be repeated for all cash flows until the present value is fully calculated.

data.content:
Finance term: annual percentage rate and,Effective annual rate (EAR)
Definition: The **annual percentage rate (APR)** is a required disclosure on nearly all consumer loans in the United States, mandated by truth-in-lending laws. However, it is often confused with the effective annual rate (EAR). When a bank quotes a car loan at 12 percent APR, it does not mean the consumer is actually paying 12 percent interest. The APR is calculated as the interest rate per period multiplied by the number of periods in a year. For instance, if a bank charges 1.2 percent per month, the APR is 1.2% × 12 = 14.4%. Therefore, an APR of 12 percent corresponds to a monthly interest rate of 1 percent. The calculation for EAR in this scenario is:

\[
\text{EAR} = [1 + (\text{APR}/12)]^{12} - 1 = 1.01^{12} - 1 = 12.6825\%
\]

Despite being called an annual rate, the APR can mislead consumers about the actual cost of borrowing. Moreover, truth-in-saving laws require institutions to disclose an "annual percentage yield" (APY) for savings accounts, which is in fact an EAR. This discrepancy means that borrowers (APRs) and savers (APYs) are not provided the same type of rate.

A significant difference arises between APR and EAR, particularly with high-interest loans like **payday loans**. These short-term loans typically last less than two weeks. In an example from AmeriCash Advance, a consumer writes a postdated check for $125, receiving $100 immediately. The interest rate for 15 days can be calculated using the future value (FV) equation:

\[
\text{FV} = \text{PV} \times (1 + r)^{\text{t}}
\]

Substituting in the known values:

\[
125 = 100 \times (1 + r)^{1} \implies 1.25 = (1 + r) \implies r = 0.25 \text{ or } 25\%
\]

This 25% is the interest for just 15 days. The APR becomes:

\[
\text{APR} = .25 \times (365/15) = 6.08333 \text{ or } 608.33\%
\]

The EAR for this payday loan can be calculated as follows:

\[
\text{EAR} = (1 + \text{Quoted rate}/m)^{\text{w}} - 1 = (1 + .25)^{w/3} - 1 \implies \text{EAR} = 227.1096 \text{ or } 22,710.96\%
\]

National Payday allows a similar loan but extends the repayment period to 18 days. The APR for this arrangement is calculated to be 506.94 percent, leading to an EAR of 9,128.26 percent.

In summary, consumers should exercise caution when interpreting APR and EAR, especially concerning high-interest loans, as the actual costs can be significantly higher than what APR figures suggest.

Finance term: Call option
Definition: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset by a certain date for a certain price.
Consider the situation of an investor who buys a European call option with a strike price of $100 to purchase 100 shares of a certain stock. Suppose that the current stock price is $98, the expiration date of the option is in 4 months, and the price of an option to purchase one share is $5. The initial investment is $500. Because the option is European, the investor can exercise only on the expiration date. If the stock price on this date is less than $100, the investor will clearly choose not to exercise. (There is no point in buying for $100 a share that has a market value of less than $100.) In these circumstances, the investor loses the whole of the initial investment of $500. If the stock price is above $100 on the expiration date, the option will be exercised. Suppose, for example, that the stock price is $115. By exercising the option, the investor is able to buy 100 shares for $100 per share. If the shares are sold immediately, the investor makes a gain of $15 per share, or $1,500, ignoring transaction costs. When the initial cost of the option is taken into account, the net profit to the investor is $1,000.\n\nFigure 10.1.1 shows how the investor's net profit or loss on an option to purchase one share varies with the final stock price in the example. For example, when the final stock price is $120, the profit from an option to purchase one share is $15. It is important to realize that an investor sometimes exercises an option and makes a loss overall. Suppose that, in the example, the stock price is $102 at the expiration of the option. The investor would exercise for a gain of \\(\\$102-\\$100=\\$2\\) and realize a loss overall of $3 when the initial cost of the option is taken into account. It is tempting to argue that the investor should not exercise the option in these circumstances. However, not exercising would lead to a loss of $5, which is worse than the $3 loss when the investor exercises. In general, call options should always be exercised at the expiration date if the stock price is above the strike price.
