data.content:
Finance term: stop-loss strategy,Hedging
Definition: A stop-loss strategy is a hedging procedure applied by institutions that have written a call option with a strike price \(K\) to purchase one unit of stock. The strategy involves buying the stock when its price rises above \(K\) and selling it when it falls below \(K\). The goal is to maintain a naked position when the stock price is less than \(K\) and a covered position when it exceeds \(K\). This method is designed to ensure that by time \(T\), the institution will own the stock if the option closes in the money and will not own it if the option closes out of the money.

The initial cost of implementing the hedge is \(S_{0}\) if \(S_{0}>K\) and zero otherwise. The total cost \(Q\) of writing and hedging the option appears to equate to the option's initial intrinsic value:

\[
Q=\max(S_{0}-K,\;0) \tag{11}
\]

Assuming no transaction costs, this would suggest that the hedging procedure works efficiently. Moreover, it implies that the hedging cost is always less than the Black-Scholes-Merton price, creating an opportunity for riskless profit by writing options and hedging them.

However, there are two critical reasons why equation (11) is incorrect. First, cash flows for the hedger occur at different times and need to be discounted. Second, purchases and sales cannot be executed at the same price \(K\). In efficient markets, hedgers cannot predict whether the stock price will remain above or drop below \(K\) when it reaches that level. Therefore, actual purchases must occur at \(K+\epsilon\) and sales at \(K-\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is a small positive number. This means every buy and sell transaction incurs an additional cost of \(2\epsilon\).

In an effort to mitigate costs, hedgers may choose to monitor price movements more closely, thus reducing \(\epsilon\). However, as \(\epsilon\) approaches zero, the frequency of trades increases, leading to a trade-off between lower costs per transaction and higher overall trading volume. Consequently, as \(\epsilon\to 0\), the expected number of trades tends toward infinity.

While the stop-loss strategy may appear appealing, its effectiveness as a hedging mechanism is questionable, particularly for out-of-the-money options. If the stock price doesn't reach the strike price \(K\), hedging costs remain zero. Conversely, if the price fluctuates around \(K\), the strategy can become expensive. Monte Carlo simulations can evaluate the strategy's overall performance by sampling various stock price paths and reviewing the outcomes. The performance measure for hedging, shown in Table 19.1, is the ratio of the standard deviation of hedging costs to the Black-Scholes-Merton price. A robust hedging scheme should yield a measure close to zero; however, in this case, it remains above 0.7 regardless of how small \(\Delta t\) is, thereby indicating that the stop-loss strategy is not an effective hedging procedure.

\centering
\caption{Performance of stop-loss strategy. The performance measure is the ratio of the standard deviation of the cost of writing the option and hedging it to the theoretical price of the option.}
\begin{tabular}{c|cccccc}
\hline
$\Delta t$ (weeks) & 5    & 4    & 2    & 1    & 0.5  & 0.25 \\ \hline
Hedge performance   & 0.98 & 0.93 & 0.83 & 0.79 & 0.77 & 0.76 \\ 
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Finance term: Zions Bancorp,Employee stock option
Definition: One way of valuing an employee stock option is to see what the market would pay for it. Cisco was the first to try this in 2006. It proposed selling options with the exact terms of its employee stock options to institutional investors. This approach was rejected by the SEC on the grounds that the range of investors bidding for the options was not wide enough.

Zions Bancorp has suggested an alternative approach. It proposed that securities providing payoffs mirroring those actually realized by its employees be sold. Suppose that the strike price for a particular grant to employees is $40 and it turns out that 1% of employees exercise after exactly 5 years when the stock price is $60, 2% exercise after exactly 6 years when the stock price is $65, and so on. Then 1% of the securities owned by an investor will provide a $20 payoff after 5 years, 2% will provide a payoff of $25 after 6 years, and so on.

Zions Bancorp tested the idea using its own stock option grant to its employees. It sold the securities using a Dutch auction process. In this individuals or companies can submit a bid indicating the price they are prepared to pay and the number of options they are prepared to buy. The clearing price is the highest bid such that the aggregate number of options sought at that price or a higher price equals or exceeds the number of options for sale. Buyers who have bid more than the clearing price get their orders filled at the clearing price and the buyer who bid the clearing price gets the remainder. Zions Bancorp announced that it had received SEC approval for its market-based approach in October 2007, but the approach has not been used to any great extent.

data.content:
Finance term: Disadvantages of Exchange-Rate Targeting,To Peg or Not to Peg: Exchange-Rate Targeting as an Alternative Monetary Policy Strategy
Definition: Despite the inherent advantages of exchange-rate targeting, there are several serious criticisms of this strategy. The problem (as we saw earlier in the chapter) is that with capital mobility the targeting country can no longer pursue its own independent monetary policy and use it to respond to domestic shocks that are independent of those hitting the anchor country. Furthermore, an exchange-rate target means that shocks to the anchor country are directly transmitted to the targeting country, because changes in interest rates in the anchor country lead to a corresponding change in interest rates in the targeting country. A second problem with exchange-rate targets is that they leave countries open to speculative attacks on their currencies.
In contrast to industrialized countries, emerging market countries (including the transition countries of Eastern Europe) may not lose much by giving up an independent monetary policy when they target exchange rates. Because many emerging market countries have not developed the political or monetary institutions that allow the successful use of discretionary monetary policy, they may have little to gain from an independent monetary policy, but a lot to lose. Thus they would be better off by, in effect, adopting the monetary policy of a country like the United States through targeting exchange rates than by pursuing their own independent policy. This is one of the reasons that so many emerging market countries have adopted exchange-rate targeting.
Nonetheless, exchange-rate targeting is highly dangerous for these countries, because it leaves them open to speculative attacks that can have far more serious consequences for their economies than for the economies of industrialized countries.
An additional disadvantage of an exchange-rate target is that it can weaken the accountability of policymakers, particularly in emerging market countries. Because exchange-rate targeting fixes the exchange rate, it eliminates an important signal that can help constrain monetary policy from becoming too expansionary and thereby limit the time-inconsistency problem. In industrialized countries, particularly in the United States, the bond market provides an important signal about the stance of monetary policy. Overly expansionary monetary policy or strong political pressure to engage in overly expansionary monetary policy produces an inflation scare in which inflation expectations surge, interest rates rise because of the Fisher effect (described in Chapter 5), and there is a sharp decline in long-term bond prices. Because both central banks and the politicians want to avoid this kind of scenario, overly expansionary monetary policy will be less likely.
In many countries, particularly emerging market countries, the long-term bond market is essentially nonexistent. Under a floating exchange rate regime, however, if monetary policy is too expansionary, the exchange rate will depreciate. In these countries the daily fluctuations of the exchange rate can, like the bond market in the United States, provide an early warning signal that monetary policy is too expansionary. Just as the fear of a visible inflation scare in the bond market constrains central bankers from pursuing overly expansionary monetary policy and constrains politicians from putting pressure on the central bank to engage in overly expansionary monetary policy, fear of exchange-rate depreciations can make overly expansionary monetary policy, and the time-inconsistency problem, less likely.

options.A: They have robust political and monetary institutions
options.B: They have weak political or monetary institutions
options.C: They have strong trade agreements with other countries

A second problem with exchange-rate targets is that they leave countries open to speculative attacks on their currencies.
In contrast to industrialized countries, emerging market countries (including the transition countries of Eastern Europe) may not lose much by giving up an independent monetary policy when they target exchange rates. Because many emerging market countries have not developed the political or monetary institutions that allow the successful use of discretionary monetary policy, they may have little to gain from an independent monetary policy, but a lot to lose. Thus they would be better off by, in effect, adopting the monetary policy of a country like the United States through targeting exchange rates than by pursuing their own independent policy. This is one of the reasons that so many emerging market countries have adopted exchange-rate targeting.
Nonetheless, exchange-rate targeting is highly dangerous for these countries, because it leaves them open to speculative attacks that can have far more serious consequences for their economies than for the economies of industrialized countries.
An additional disadvantage of an exchange-rate target is that it can weaken the accountability of policymakers, particularly in emerging market countries. Because exchange-rate targeting fixes the exchange rate, it eliminates an important signal that can help constrain monetary policy from becoming too expansionary and thereby limit the time-inconsistency problem. In industrialized countries, particularly in the United States, the bond market provides an important signal about the stance of monetary policy. Overly expansionary monetary policy or strong political pressure to engage in overly expansionary monetary policy produces an inflation scare in which inflation expectations surge, interest rates rise because of the Fisher effect (described in Chapter 5), and there is a sharp decline in long-term bond prices. Because both central banks and the politicians want to avoid this kind of scenario, overly expansionary monetary policy will be less likely.
In many countries, particularly emerging market countries, the long-term bond market is essentially nonexistent. Under a floating exchange rate regime, however, if monetary policy is too expansionary, the exchange rate will depreciate. In these countries the daily fluctuations of the exchange rate can, like the bond market in the United States, provide an early warning signal that monetary policy is too expansionary. Just as the fear of a visible inflation scare in the bond market constrains central bankers from pursuing overly expansionary monetary policy and constrains politicians from putting pressure on the central bank to engage in overly expansionary monetary policy, fear of exchange-rate depreciations can make overly expansionary monetary policy, and the time-inconsistency problem, less likely.

question:
Employee stock options and exchange-traded call options on non-dividend-paying stocks have different exercise behaviors.Why is an exchange-traded call option on a non-dividend-paying stock never exercised early?

Options:
A. Exchange-traded call options expire earlier than employee stock options
B. Exchange-traded call options have a higher intrinsic value when exercised early
C. It is always more beneficial for the option holder to sell the call option rather than exercise it
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: early exercise of,Employee stock option
Definition: The fourth feature of employee stock option plans noted above has important implications. If employees, for whatever reason, want to realize a cash benefit from options that have vested, they must exercise the options and sell the underlying shares. They cannot sell the options to someone else. This leads to a tendency for employee stock options to be exercised earlier than similar exchange-traded or over-the-counter call options.

Consider a call option on a stock paying no dividends. In Section 11.5 we showed that, if it is a regular call option, it should never be exercised early. The holder of the option will always do better by selling the option rather than exercising it before the end of its life. However, the arguments we used in Section 11.5 are not applicable to employee stock options because they cannot be sold. The only way employees can realize a cash benefit from the options (or diversify their holdings) is by exercising the options and selling the stock. It is therefore not unusual for an employee stock option to be exercised well before it would be optimal to exercise the option if it were a regular exchange-traded or over-the-counter option.

Should an employee ever exercise his or her options before maturity and then keep the stock rather than selling it? Assume that the option's strike price is constant during the life of the option and the option can be exercised at any time. To answer the question we consider two options: the employee stock option and an otherwise identical regular option that can be sold in the market. We refer to the first option as option A and the second as option B. If the stock pays no dividends, we know that option B should never be exercised early. It follows that it is not optimal to exercise option A and keep the stock. If the employee wants to maintain a stake in his or her company, a better strategy is to keep the option. This delays paying the strike price and maintains the insurance value of the option, as described in Section 11.5. Only when it is optimal to exercise option B can it be a rational strategy for an employee to exercise option A before maturity and keep the stock.1 As discussed in Section 15.12, it is optimal to exercise option B only when a relatively high dividend is imminent.

Footnote 1: The only exception to this could be when an executive wants to own the stock for its voting rights.

In practice the early exercise behavior of employees varies widely from company to company. In some companies, there is a culture of not exercising early; in others, employees tend to exercise options and sell the stock soon after the end of the vesting period, even if the options are only slightly in the money.

The too-big-to-fail policy remains a controversial topic in banking regulation, discussing both potential benefits and significant drawbacks.Which one of the following benefits is provided by a too-big-to-fail policy?

data.content:
Finance term: Financial Consolidation and the Government Safety Net,Government Safety Net,Asymmetric Information and Financial Regulation
Definition: Financial consolidation poses two challenges to financial regulation because of the existence of the government safety net. First, the increased size of financial institutions as a result of financial consolidation increases the too-big-to-fail problem, because there will now be more large institutions whose failure would expose the financial system to systemic (systemwide) risk. Thus more financial institutions are likely to be treated as too big to fail, and the increased moral hazard incentives for these large institutions to take on greater risk can then increase the fragility of the financial system. Second, financial consolidation of banks with other financial services firms means that the government safety net may be extended to new activities such as securities underwriting, insurance, or real estate activities, as has occurred during the subprime financial crisis in 2008. This increases incentives for greater risk taking in these activities that can also weaken the fabric of the financial system. Limiting the moral hazard incentives for the larger, more complex financial organizations that have arisen as a result of recent changes in legislation will be one of the key issues facing banking regulators in the aftermath of the subprime financial crisis.

question:
The efficient market hypothesis implies that high costs of managing a portfolio can be a challenge for small investors.Which one of the following strategies is frequently sensible for a small investor according to the efficient market hypothesis?

Options:
A. Invest in individual stocks with high brokerage commissions
B. Choose mutual funds with high management fees
C. Buy into a low-fee, commission-free mutual fund
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: efficient market hypothesis,The Efficient Market Hypothesis: Rational Expectations in Financial Markets
Definition: The efficient market hypothesis is based on the assumption that prices of securities in financial markets fully reflect all available information. Recall that the rate of return from holding a security equals the sum of the capital gain on the security (the change in the price), plus any cash payments, divided by the initial purchase price of the security:
R = \frac{P_{t + 1} - P_{t} + C}{P_{t}}
where 
R = rate of return on the security held from time t to t+1 (say, the end of 2010 to the end of 2011)
P_{t+1} = price of the security at time t+1, the end of the holding period 
P_{t} = price of the security at time t, the beginning of the holding period 
C = cash payment (coupon or dividend payments) made in the period t to t+1
Let's look at the expectation of this return at time t, the beginning of the holding period. Because the current price P_{t} and the cash payment C are known at the beginning, the only variable in the definition of the return that is uncertain is the price next period, P_{t+1}. Denoting the expectation of the security's price at the end of the holding period as P_{t+1}^{e}, the expected return R^{e} is
R^{e} = P_{t+1}^{e} - P_{t} + C
The efficient market hypothesis views expectations of future prices as equal to optimal forecasts using all currently available information. In other words, the markets expectations of future securities prices are rational, so that
P_{t+1}^{e} = P_{t+1}^{of}
which in turn implies that the expected return on the security will equal the optimal forecast of the return:
R^{e} = R^{of}
Unfortunately, we cannot observe either R^{e} or P_{t+1}^{e}, so the rational expectations equations by themselves do not tell us much about how the financial market behaves. However, supply and demand analysis enables us to determine the expected return on a security using the equilibrium return R^*; this is, R^e=R^*. Replacing R^e with R^*, we get R^{of}=R^*.
Rational Behind the Hypothesis is as follows:
Denote the optimal forecast of the return and the equilibrium return as R^{of} and R^*, respectively. The rational behind the efficient market hypothesis are summarized as follows:
R_{of} > R^* --> increase in the current stock price P_t --> decrease in R_{of}
R_{of} < R^* --> decrease in the current stock price P_t --> increase in R_{of}
until R^{of}=R^*.

options.A: Invest in individual stocks with high brokerage commissions
options.B: Choose mutual funds with high management fees
options.C: Buy into a low-fee, commission-free mutual fund

question:
Friedman and Keynes had differing views on the predictability of the demand for money and, consequently, the velocity of money.What is one reason that Friedman deemed the demand for money as predictable?

Options:
A. Interest rates have large fluctuations affecting the demand for money.
B. Interest rates have only small effects on the demand for money.
C. People's expectations of interest rates change frequently.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money,Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money
Definition: The theory of asset demand suggests that the demand for money is influenced by individual wealth and the expected returns of other assets compared to the expected return on money. Friedman formulated the demand for money as follows:

\[
\frac{M^{d}}{P} = f(Y_{p}, r_{b}-r_{m}, r_{e}-r_{m}, \pi^{e}-r_{m})
\]

where:
- \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) = demand for real money balances
- \(Y_{p}\) = Friedman's measure of wealth, known as permanent income
- \(r_{m}\) = expected return on money
- \(r_{b}\) = expected return on bonds
- \(r_{e}\) = expected return on equity (common stocks)
- \(\pi^{e}\) = expected inflation rate

The demand for money \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) is positively related to permanent income \(Y_{p}\) while negatively related to the terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\), \(r_{e}-r_{m}\), and \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\). 

Permanent income is the present discounted value of expected future income, representing a long-term average that minimizes fluctuations from short-run income changes. As such, the demand for money, influenced by permanent income, remains relatively stable despite business cycle fluctuations. 

Individuals can hold wealth in several forms, categorized by Friedman into three types of assets: bonds, equity, and goods. The demand for these assets relative to money is shaped by expected returns, reflected in the latter terms of the demand function. 

The expected return on money \(r_{m}\) is determined by two factors: the services provided by banks on deposits, such as check provision or bill payments, and interest payments on money balances. An increase in either of these factors generally raises the expected return on holding money.

The terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\) and \(r_{e}-r_{m}\) compare the expected returns on bonds and equity, respectively, to money. As these terms increase, the relative attractiveness of money diminishes, leading to a decreased demand for money. Additionally, the term \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\) compares the expected return on goods (driven by capital gains from price increases, reflecting inflation) to money. An increase in this term indicates that holding goods becomes more attractive compared to money, which also results in a decreased demand for money.

Overall, Friedman's model illustrates the dynamic interplay between wealth, asset returns, and the demand for money, emphasizing the stability of money demand during economic fluctuations while highlighting how relative returns on various assets influence money-holding behaviors.

options.B: Interest rates have only small effects on the demand for money.
options.C: People's expectations of interest rates change frequently.

A. Credit unions are heavily regulated and cannot expand their services.
B. Credit unions have higher lending rates compared to other depository institutions.
C. Credit unions only have members who share a common employer or are associated with a particular organization.

data.content:
Finance term: Credit Unions,Thrift Industry: Regulation an Structure
Definition: Credit unions are small cooperative lending institutions organized around a particular group of individuals with a common bond (e.g., union members or employees of a particular firm). They are the only depository institutions that are tax-exempt and can be chartered either by the states or by the federal government; more than half are federally chartered. The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) issues federal charters and regulates federally chartered credit unions by setting minimum capital requirements, requiring periodic reports, and examining the credit unions. Federal deposit insurance (up to the $100,000-per-account limit, temporarily $250,000) is provided to both federally chartered and state-chartered credit unions by a subsidiary of the NCUA, the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF). Because the majority of credit union lending is for consumer loans with fairly short terms to maturity, these institutions did not suffer the financial difficulties of the S&Ls and mutual savings banks.
Because their members share a common bond, credit unions are typically quite small; most hold less than $10 million of assets. In addition, their ties to a particular industry or company make them more likely to fail when large numbers of workers in that industry or company are laid off and have trouble making loan payments. Recent regulatory changes allow individual credit unions to cater to a more diverse group of people by interpreting the common bond requirement less strictly, and this has encouraged an expansion in the size of credit unions that may help reduce credit union failures in the future.
Often a credit union's shareholders are dispersed over many states, and sometimes even worldwide, so branching across state lines and into other countries is permitted for federally chartered credit unions. The Navy Federal Credit Union, for example, whose shareholders are members of the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, has branches throughout the world.

question:
In financial modeling, specific formulas are used to determine the up (\(u\)) and down (\(d\)) factors in terms of volatility.Which one of the following formulas correctly represents the up factor (\(u\)) in terms of volatility?

Options:
A. \(u = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\)
B. \(u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\)
C. \(u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\)
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: matching volatility,Binomial tree
Definition: To construct a binomial tree with a time step \( \Delta t \), three parameters are required: \( u \), \( d \), and \( p \). Once \( u \) and \( d \) are set, the probability \( p \) must ensure that the expected return is equal to the risk-free rate \( r \). The relationship is given by:

\[
p = \frac{e^{r\Delta t} - d}{u - d} \tag{13.11}
\]

Parameters \( u \) and \( d \) must align with the volatility \( \sigma \) of the asset. The volatility is defined such that the standard deviation of returns over a short period \( \Delta t \) is \( \sigma \sqrt{\Delta t} \), resulting in a variance of \( \sigma^2 \Delta t \). The variance for a variable \( X \) is defined as \( E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \), where \( E \) denotes expected value.

During a time step of length \( \Delta t \), with probability \( p \), the stock yields a return of \( u - 1 \), and with probability \( 1 - p \), it produces a return of \( d - 1 \). To match volatility, the following condition must hold:

\[
p(u - 1)^2 + (1 - p)(d - 1)^2 - [p(u - 1) + (1 - p)(d - 1)]^2 = \sigma^2 \Delta t \tag{13.12}
\]

Substituting for \( p \) from equation (13.11) simplifies to:

\[
e^{r\Delta t}(u + d) - ud - e^{2r\Delta t} = \sigma^2 \Delta t \tag{13.13}
\]

Neglecting terms of \( \Delta t^2 \) and higher, a solution to this equation is:

\[
u = e^{\sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}} \quad \text{and} \quad d = e^{-\sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}}
\]

These values align with those proposed by Cox, Ross, and Rubinstein (1979).

When matching volatility in the real world, the same formulas for \( u \) and \( d \) are maintained. Let \( p^* \) denote the probability of an up-movement in the real world and \( \mu \) be the expected return. The equation relating \( p^* \) to \( u \) and \( d \) becomes:

\[
p^* = \frac{e^{\mu \Delta t} - d}{u - d}
\]

The variance matching equation alters to:

\[
e^{\mu \Delta t}(u + d) - ud - e^{2\mu \Delta t} = \sigma^2 \Delta t
\]

This follows the same structure as equation (13.13), replacing \( r \) with \( \mu \). Again, neglecting \( \Delta t^2 \) and higher powers yields the same solution:

\[
u = e^{\sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}} \quad \text{and} \quad d = e^{-\sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}}
\] 

Thus, regardless of whether volatility is matched in the risk-neutral or real world, the derived values for \( u \) and \( d \) remain unchanged.

options.A: \(u = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\)
options.B: \(u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\)
options.C: \(u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\)

Jumps in the underlying asset price can affect the stock price distribution and create a volatility smile.Which one of the following effects do jumps in the underlying asset price have on the stock price distribution?

Options:
A. They make both tails of the stock price distribution heavier than those of the lognormal distribution
B. They make both tails of the stock price distribution lighter than those of the lognormal distribution
C. They have no effect on the stock price distribution
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: jump in asset price anticipated,Black–Scholes–Merton and volatility smile
Definition: Let us now consider an example of how an unusual volatility smile might arise in equity markets. Suppose that a stock price is currently $50 and an important news announcement due in a few days is expected either to increase the stock price by $8 or to reduce it by $8. (This announcement could concern the outcome of a takeover attempt or the verdict in an important lawsuit.) The probability distribution of the stock price in, say, 1 month might then consist of a mixture of two lognormal distributions, the first corresponding to favorable news, the second to unfavorable news. The situation is illustrated in Figure 20.5. The solid line shows the mixture-of-lognormals distribution for the stock price in 1 month; the dashed line shows a lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as this distribution.\n\nThe true probability distribution is bimodal (certainly not lognormal). One easy way to investigate the general effect of a bimodal stock price distribution is to consider the extreme case where there are only two possible future stock prices. This is what we will now do.\n\nSuppose that the stock price is currently $50 and that it is known that in 1 month it will be either $42 or $58. Suppose further that the risk-free rate is 12% per annum. The situation is illustrated in Figure 20.6. Options can be valued using the binomial model from Chapter 13. In this case \\(u=1.16\\), \\(d=0.84\\), \\(a=1.0101\\), and \\(p=0.5314\\). The results from valuing a range of different options are shown in Table 20.3. The first column shows alternative strike prices; the second column shows prices of 1-month European call options; the third column shows the prices of one-month European put option prices; the fourth column shows implied volatilities. (As shown in Section 20.1, the implied volatility of a European put option is the same as that of a European call option when they have the same strike price and maturity.) Figure 20.7 displays the volatility smile from Table 20.3. It is actually a \"frown\" (the opposite of that observed for currencies) with volatilities declining as we move out of or into the money. The volatility implied from an option with a strike price of 50 will overprice an option with a strike price of 44 or 56.

    \caption{Implied volatilities in situation where it is known that the stock price will move from \$50 to either \$42 or \$58.}
    \begin{tabular}{cccc}
        \hline
        Strike price & Call price & Put price & Implied volatility \\
        (\$) & (\$) & (\$) & (\%) \\
        \hline

        44  & 7.37  & 0.93  & 58.8  \\
        46  & 6.31  & 1.86  & 66.6  \\

        54  & 2.10  & 5.57  & 60.0  \\
        56  & 1.05  & 6.50  & 49.0  \\
        58  & 0.00  & 7.42  & 0.0  \\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The FDICIA legislation introduced measures to limit the too-big-to-fail policy.Which one of the following changes to the FDICIA legislation likely increases the safety of the banking system?

A. The FDIC must increase deposit insurance limits for large banks.

instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Financial Consolidation and the Government Safety Net,Government Safety Net,Asymmetric Information and Financial Regulation
Definition: Financial consolidation poses two challenges to financial regulation because of the existence of the government safety net. First, the increased size of financial institutions as a result of financial consolidation increases the too-big-to-fail problem, because there will now be more large institutions whose failure would expose the financial system to systemic (systemwide) risk. Thus more financial institutions are likely to be treated as too big to fail, and the increased moral hazard incentives for these large institutions to take on greater risk can then increase the fragility of the financial system. Second, financial consolidation of banks with other financial services firms means that the government safety net may be extended to new activities such as securities underwriting, insurance, or real estate activities, as has occurred during the subprime financial crisis in 2008. This increases incentives for greater risk taking in these activities that can also weaken the fabric of the financial system. Limiting the moral hazard incentives for the larger, more complex financial organizations that have arisen as a result of recent changes in legislation will be one of the key issues facing banking regulators in the aftermath of the subprime financial crisis.

Finance term: valuation Black-Scholes,Currency option
Definition: To value currency options, the spot exchange rate, S_{0}, is defined as the value of one unit of foreign currency in US dollars. A foreign currency acts similarly to a stock that pays a known dividend yield; the yield for the owner of the foreign currency is equal to the foreign risk-free interest rate, r_{f}. 

European call and put option prices are bounded as follows:

\[
c \geqslant\max\bigl{(}S_{0}e^{-r_{f}T}-Ke^{-rT},\,0\bigr{)}
\]

\[
p \geqslant\max\bigl{(}Ke^{-rT}-S_{0}e^{-r_{f}T},\,0\bigr{)}
\]

The put-call parity for European currency options is given by:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_{0}e^{-r_{f}T}
\]

The pricing formulas for European currency options are described by:

\[
c = S_{0}e^{-r_{f}T}N(d_{1}) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_{2}) \tag{17.11}
\]

\[
p = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_{2}) - S_{0}e^{-r_{f}T}N(-d_{1}) \tag{17.12}
\]

where:

\[
d_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K) + (r - r_{f} + \sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]

\[
d_{2} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K) + (r - r_{f} - \sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} = d_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T}
\]

Both domestic interest rate, r, and foreign interest rate, r_{f}, are applicable for maturity T.

The relationship between put and call options on currency indicates symmetry; a put option to sell one unit of currency A for currency B at strike price K is equivalent to a call option to buy K units of B with currency A at strike price 1/K.

Forward exchange rates, actively traded by banks and other financial institutions, are frequently utilized for valuing options. The forward rate, F_{0}, for maturity T is defined as:

\[
F_{0} = S_{0}e^{(r - r_{f})T}
\]

This allows the European option pricing formulas to be simplified to:

\[
c = e^{-rT}[F_{0}N(d_{1}) - KN(d_{2})] \tag{17.13}
\]

\[
p = e^{-rT}[KN(-d_{2}) - F_{0}N(-d_{1})] \tag{17.14}
\]

Where the updated definitions for d_{1} and d_{2} are:

\[
d_{1} = \frac{\ln(F_{0}/K) + \sigma^{2}T/2}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]

\[
d_{2} = \frac{\ln(F_{0}/K) - \sigma^{2}T/2}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} = d_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T}
\]

Equations (17.13) and (17.14) align with previous formulations, demonstrating that a European option based on the spot price of an asset can be valued in terms of the forward or futures contract price, provided their maturities are the same.

question:
It is sometimes argued that a forward exchange rate can predict future exchange rates accurately.Which one of the following describes a circumstance in which the forward exchange rate is an unbiased predictor of the future exchange rate?

Options:
A. The exchange rate has no systematic risk.
B. The exchange rate is highly volatile.
C. The exchange rate is influenced by external factors.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: risk and return,Futures contract
Definition: A speculator takes a long position in a futures contract lasting for \\(T\\) years, aiming for the spot price of the asset to exceed the futures price at contract expiration. Ignoring daily settlement, the futures contract is treated like a forward contract. The speculator invests the present value of the futures price in a risk-free investment, using the proceeds to buy the asset upon maturity. The cash flows for the speculator are outlined as follows:

Today: \(-F_{0}e^{-rT}\)

End of futures contract: \(+S_{T}\)

where \\(F_{0}\\) is the current futures price, \\(S_{T}\\) is the asset price at time \\(T\\), and \\(r\\) represents the risk-free return over time \\(T\\).

To value this investment, the appropriate discount rate for the expected cash flow at time \\(T\\) equals an investor's required return, denoted as \\(k\\). The present value of the investment can thus be expressed as:

\[-F_{0}e^{-rT}+E(S_{T})e^{-kT}\\]

Assuming all investments are priced with zero net present value leads to the equation:

\[-F_{0}e^{-rT}+E(S_{T})e^{-kT}=0\\]

which simplifies to:

\[F_{0}=E(S_{T})e^{(r-k)T} \\tag{5.20}\\]

The required returns on investments depend on their systematic risk. For an investment in the asset underlying the futures contract, if returns are uncorrelated with the stock market, then \\(k=r\\), resulting in:

\[F_{0}=E(S_{T})\\]

This demonstrates that the futures price serves as an unbiased estimate of the expected future spot price under these conditions.

Conversely, if the asset's return is positively correlated with the stock market, then \\(k>r\\). This indicates that:

\[F_{0}<E(S_{T})\\]

Thus, when the asset has positive systematic risk, the futures price likely understates the expected future spot price. A typical example of this scenario is a stock index, where returns generally surpass the risk-free rate, \\(r\\), factoring in dividends that yield \\(q\\), leading to an increase in the index greater than \\(r-q\\).

In the case of negative correlation with the stock market, where \\(k<r\\), it yields:

\[F_{0}>E(S_{T})\\]

This implies that with negative systematic risk, the futures price tends to overstate the expected future spot price. 

These results are concisely summarized, illustrating the relationship between futures prices, expected spot price, and systematic risk within the financial market context.
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Relationship between futures price and expected future spot price.}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\textbf{Underlying asset} & \textbf{Relationship of expected return k from asset to risk-free rate r} & \textbf{Relationship of futures price F to expected future spot price E($S_T$)} \\ \hline
No systematic risk & $k = r$ & $F_0 = E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
Positive systematic risk & $k > r$ & $F_0 < E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
Negative systematic risk & $k < r$ & $F_0 > E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

An up-and-out barrier call option on a non-dividend-paying stock with specific parameters such as a stock price of 50, strike price of 50, volatility of 30%, risk-free rate of 5%, one-year maturity, and a barrier at $80 is valued.What happens to the delta of an up-and-out barrier call option when the stock price exceeds $57?

Options:
A. Delta remains constant
B. Delta becomes negative
C. Delta becomes positive
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: barrier options,Exotic options
Definition: Barrier options are financial derivatives whose payoffs depend on whether the price of an underlying asset reaches a specific level during a defined time frame. They are commonly traded in the over-the-counter market and are popular due to their lower costs compared to standard options. These options are categorized into two main types: knock-out options and knock-in options. Knock-out options become void if the underlying asset’s price breaches a barrier, while knock-in options only take effect when a barrier is crossed.

The values of regular call and put options at time zero are given by:

\[
c = S_{0}e^{-qT}N(d_{1}) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_{2})
\]
\[
p = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_{2}) - S_{0}e^{-qT}N(-d_{1})
\]

where

\[
d_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K)+(r-q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]
\[
d_{2} = d_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T}
\]

A down-and-out call is a type of knock-out option that becomes worthless if the asset price hits a barrier level \(H\), which is set below the initial asset price. Correspondingly, a down-and-in call only becomes effective if the price reaches this barrier. When \(H \leq K\), the value of a down-and-in call at time zero is calculated as:

\[
c_{\text{di}} = S_{0}e^{-qT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda}N(y) - Ke^{-rT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda - 2}N(y - \sigma\sqrt{T})
\]

with \(\lambda = \frac{r-q+\sigma^{2}/2}{\sigma^{2}}\) and \(y = \frac{\ln[H^{2}/(S_{0}K)]}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} + \lambda\sigma\sqrt{T}\).

The value of a down-and-out call is then given by:

\[
c_{\rm do} = c - c_{\rm di}
\]

For scenarios where \(H \geq K\):

\[
c_{\rm do} = S_{0}N(x_{1})e^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}N(x_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T}) - S_{0}e^{-qT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda}N(y_{1}) + Ke^{-rT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda - 2}N(y_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T})
\]

The corresponding knock-in value is \(c_{\rm di} = c - c_{\rm do}\) with 

\[
x_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/H)}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} + \lambda\sigma\sqrt{T}, \quad y_{1} = \frac{\ln(H/S_{0})}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} + \lambda\sigma\sqrt{T}
\]

Up-and-out and up-and-in options similarly follow these principles, affected by the barrier \(H\) in relation to the strike price \(K\). 

Put barrier options operate analogously. An up-and-out put ceases when a barrier \(H\) that exceeds the current price is reached. Their pricing is given by:

When \(H \geq K\):

\[
p_{\rm ui} = -S_{0}e^{-qT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda}N(-y) + Ke^{-rT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda - 2}N(-y + \sigma\sqrt{T})
\]
\[
p_{\rm uo} = p - p_{\rm ui}
\]

When \(H \leq K\):

\[
p_{\rm uo} = -S_{0}N(-x_{1})e^{-qT} + Ke^{-rT}N(-x_{1} + \sigma\sqrt{T}) + S_{0}e^{-qT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda}N(-y_{1}) - Ke^{-rT}(H/S_{0})^{2\lambda - 2}N(-y_{1} + \sigma\sqrt{T})
\]
\[
p_{\rm ui} = p - p_{\rm uo}
\]

Significantly, the valuation of barrier options assumes a lognormal distribution for asset prices. The observations for whether a barrier has been breached can occur continuously or at discrete intervals, leading to adjustments in barrier levels to account for frequency of observations. 

These options also behave distinctively compared to regular options, exemplified by instances of negative vega. Finally, Parisian options represent an alternative where the asset price must remain beyond a barrier for a specified duration before being knocked in or out, complicating their valuation further and often requiring methods like Monte Carlo simulations for accurate pricing.

options.A: Delta remains constant
options.B: Delta becomes negative
options.C: Delta becomes positive

question:
The Black-Scholes-Merton price of an out-of-the-money call option with an exercise price of $40 is $4. A trader who has written this option plans to use a stop-loss strategy.Which one of the following strategies will cost the trader 0.10 each time the stock is bought or sold?

Options:
A. Buy at $40.10 and sell at $39.90
B. Buy at $41.00 and sell at $39.00
C. Buy at $39.50 and sell at $40.50
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: stop-loss strategy,Hedging
Definition: A stop-loss strategy is a hedging procedure applied by institutions that have written a call option with a strike price \(K\) to purchase one unit of stock. The strategy involves buying the stock when its price rises above \(K\) and selling it when it falls below \(K\). The goal is to maintain a naked position when the stock price is less than \(K\) and a covered position when it exceeds \(K\). This method is designed to ensure that by time \(T\), the institution will own the stock if the option closes in the money and will not own it if the option closes out of the money.

The initial cost of implementing the hedge is \(S_{0}\) if \(S_{0}>K\) and zero otherwise. The total cost \(Q\) of writing and hedging the option appears to equate to the option's initial intrinsic value:

\[
Q=\max(S_{0}-K,\;0) \tag{11}
\]

Assuming no transaction costs, this would suggest that the hedging procedure works efficiently. Moreover, it implies that the hedging cost is always less than the Black-Scholes-Merton price, creating an opportunity for riskless profit by writing options and hedging them.

However, there are two critical reasons why equation (11) is incorrect. First, cash flows for the hedger occur at different times and need to be discounted. Second, purchases and sales cannot be executed at the same price \(K\). In efficient markets, hedgers cannot predict whether the stock price will remain above or drop below \(K\) when it reaches that level. Finance term: non-dividend-paying stock,Binomial tree
Definition: The binomial tree valuation approach divides the life of an option into small time intervals of length \(\Delta t\), where the price of the underlying asset can move to one of two values, \(Su\) or \(Sd\). Here, \(u > 1\) indicates an "up" movement and \(d < 1\) a "down" movement. The probability of an up movement is denoted by \(p\), while the probability of a down movement is \(1-p\).

### Risk-Neutral Valuation

The risk-neutral valuation principle allows for the valuation of derivatives under the assumption that expected returns from all traded assets equal the risk-free interest rate. This involves the following steps:

1. Assume the expected return from all assets is the risk-free interest rate, \(r\).
2. Value derivative payoffs by calculating their expected values and discounting them at the risk-free rate.

### Determination of \(p\), \(u\), and \(d\)

To maintain correct mean and variance for asset price changes during the interval \(\Delta t\), the expected return from the asset, taking into account its yield \(q\), is \(r - q\). Hence, the expected asset price at time \(\Delta t\) is given by:

\[
Se^{(r-q)\Delta t} = pSu + (1-p)Sd
\]

This simplifies to:

\[
e^{(r-q)\Delta t} = pu + (1-p)d \tag{21.1}
\]

The variance of the variable \(R\) (percentage change in asset price) becomes:

\[
pu^{2} + (1-p)d^{2} - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t}
\]

Since variance is unaffected by constants, we have \(\sigma^{2}\Delta t\) as the variance of \(R\):

\[
pu^{2} + (1-p)d^{2} - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t} = \sigma^{2}\Delta t
\]

From these, employing \(u = 1/d\) leads to the equations:

\[
e^{(r-q)\Delta t}(u + d) - ud - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t} = \sigma^{2}\Delta t \tag{21.2}
\]

A solution yields:

\[
p = \frac{a - d}{u - d} \tag{21.4}
\]
\[
u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{21.5}
\]
\[
d = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{21.6}
\]
\[
a = e^{(r - q)\Delta t} \tag{21.7}
\]

### Tree of Asset Prices

At time \(0\), the asset price \(S_0\) is known. The binomial model generates a price tree, with possible prices at each node calculated as:

\[
S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j}, \quad j=0, 1, \ldots, i
\]

The tree structure ensures recombination, meaning a path that results in the same price can come from different up and down movements.

### Working Backward through the Tree

The option valuation starts at expiration (time \(T\)), where a call option is valued as \(\max(S_{T} - K, 0)\) and a put option as \(\max(K - S_{T}, 0)\). The value of the option at prior nodes is determined by risk-neutral expectations.

For an American option, early exercise potential is checked:

For a call:

\[
f_{i,j} = \max\{S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j} - K, e^{-r\Delta t}[pf_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)f_{i+1,j}]\}
\]

For a put:

\[
f_{i,j} = \max\{K - S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j}, e^{-r\Delta t}[pf_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)f_{i+1,j}]\}
\]

### Estimating Delta and Other Greek Letters

Delta (\(\Delta\)) is calculated as:

\[
\Delta = \frac{f_{1,1} - f_{1,0}}{S_{0}u - S_{0}d} \tag{21.8}
\]

Gamma (\(\Gamma\)) and theta (\(\Theta\)) can also be derived through respective changes in values across time steps. Vega (\(\mathcal{V}\)) and rho can be estimated similarly.

data.content:
Finance term: effect on VaR estimates,Gamma
Definition: The application of linear models to portfolios that include options is considered, starting with a portfolio of options on a single stock priced at S. The delta of the position, denoted as \(\delta\), reflects the rate of change of the portfolio value with respect to stock price, formulated as:

\[
\delta=\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta S}
\]
or equivalently,

\[
\Delta P=\delta\,\Delta S
\]

Here, \(\Delta S\) represents the dollar change in stock price over one day. Let \(\Delta x\) denote the percentage change in stock price:

\[
\Delta x=\frac{\Delta S}{S}
\]

From this, an approximate relationship between \(\Delta P\) and \(\Delta x\) can be established:

\[
\Delta P=S\delta\,\Delta x
\]

In scenarios with multiple underlying market variables that involve options, a linear approximation gives:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}
\]

where \(S_{i}\) is the value of the ith market variable and \(\delta_{i}\) is the delta of the portfolio related to that variable. This leads to the use of equations (22.1) for calculating the standard deviation of \(\Delta P\).

The linear model serves as an approximation and does not factor in the gamma of the portfolio, which measures the curvature of the relationship between portfolio value and underlying market variables. Gamma is defined as the rate of change of delta with respect to the market variable. Positive gamma portfolios result in positively skewed probability distributions, while negative gamma portfolios result in negatively skewed distributions.

The Value at Risk (VaR) for a portfolio is sensitive to the left tail of its probability distribution. For a 99% confidence level, the VaR represents the value below which 1% of the distribution lies. Positive gamma portfolios generally have a lighter left tail compared to normal distributions, leading to overestimation of VaR. Conversely, negative gamma portfolios typically exhibit a heavier left tail, resulting in underestimation of VaR.

For a more precise VaR estimate, both delta and gamma should relate \(\Delta P\) to \(\Delta x_{i}\). For a portfolio linked to a single asset, the relationship is expressed as:

\[
\Delta P=\delta\,\Delta S+\tfrac{1}{2}\gamma(\Delta S)^{2}
\]

With the substitution \(\Delta x=\frac{\Delta S}{S}\), it simplifies to:

\[
\Delta P=S\delta\,\Delta x+\tfrac{1}{2}S^{2}\gamma(\Delta x)^{2}
\]

For portfolios with n underlying market variables, the equation expands to:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{1}{2} S_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}\,(\Delta x_{i})^{2}
\]

where \(\delta_{i}\) and \(\gamma_{i}\) are the delta and gamma with respect to the ith market variable. In cases where individual instruments depend on multiple variables, the equation takes the form:

\[
\Delta P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\delta_{i}\,\Delta x_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}S_{i}S_{j}\gamma_{ij}\,\Delta x_{i}\,\Delta x_{j}
\]

with the "cross gamma" defined as:

\[
\gamma_{ij}=\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial S_{i}\,\partial S_{j}}
\]

While equation (22.7) is more complex, it provides a means to calculate moments for \(\Delta P\). The Cornish-Fisher expansion can subsequently estimate the percentiles of the probability distribution based on those moments.

data.content:
Finance term: Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money,Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money
Definition: The theory of asset demand suggests that the demand for money is influenced by individual wealth and the expected returns of other assets compared to the expected return on money. Friedman formulated the demand for money as follows:

\[
\frac{M^{d}}{P} = f(Y_{p}, r_{b}-r_{m}, r_{e}-r_{m}, \pi^{e}-r_{m})
\]

where:
- \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) = demand for real money balances
- \(Y_{p}\) = Friedman's measure of wealth, known as permanent income
- \(r_{m}\) = expected return on money
- \(r_{b}\) = expected return on bonds
- \(r_{e}\) = expected return on equity (common stocks)
- \(\pi^{e}\) = expected inflation rate

The demand for money \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) is positively related to permanent income \(Y_{p}\) while negatively related to the terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\), \(r_{e}-r_{m}\), and \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\). 

Permanent income is the present discounted value of expected future income, representing a long-term average that minimizes fluctuations from short-run income changes. As such, the demand for money, influenced by permanent income, remains relatively stable despite business cycle fluctuations. 

Individuals can hold wealth in several forms, categorized by Friedman into three types of assets: bonds, equity, and goods. The demand for these assets relative to money is shaped by expected returns, reflected in the latter terms of the demand function. 

The expected return on money \(r_{m}\) is determined by two factors: the services provided by banks on deposits, such as check provision or bill payments, and interest payments on money balances. An increase in either of these factors generally raises the expected return on holding money.

The terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\) and \(r_{e}-r_{m}\) compare the expected returns on bonds and equity, respectively, to money. As these terms increase, the relative attractiveness of money diminishes, leading to a decreased demand for money. Additionally, the term \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\) compares the expected return on goods (driven by capital gains from price increases, reflecting inflation) to money. An increase in this term indicates that holding goods becomes more attractive compared to money, which also results in a decreased demand for money.

Overall, Friedman's model illustrates the dynamic interplay between wealth, asset returns, and the demand for money, emphasizing the stability of money demand during economic fluctuations while highlighting how relative returns on various assets influence money-holding behaviors.

data.content:
Finance term: basic idea,Net present value (NPV)
Definition: An investment is worth undertaking if it creates value for its owners. In the most general sense, we create value by identifying an investment worth more in the marketplace than it costs us to acquire. How can something be worth more than it costs? It's a case of the whole being worth more than the cost of the parts.

For example, suppose you buy a run-down house for $25,000 and spend another $25,000 on painters, plumbers, and so on to get it fixed up. Your total investment is $50,000. When the work is completed, you place the house back on the market and find that it's worth $60,000. The market value ($60,000) exceeds the cost ($50,000) by $10,000. What you have done here is to act as a manager and bring together some fixed assets (a house), some labor (plumbers, carepners, and others), and some materials (carpeting, paint, and so on). The net result is that you have created $10,000 in value. Put another way, this $10,000 is the _value added_ by management.

With our house example, it turned out _after the fact_ that $10,000 in value had been created. Things thus worked out nicely. The real challenge, of course, would have been to somehow identify _ahead of time_ whether investing the necessary $50,000 was a good idea in the first place. This is what capital budgeting is all about--namely, trying to determine whether a proposed investment or project will be worth more, once it is in place, than it costs.

For reasons that will be obvious in a moment, the difference between an investment's market value and its cost is called the **net present value** of the investment, abbreviated **NPV**. In other words, net present value is a measure of how much value is created or added today by undertaking an investment. Given our goal of creating value for the stockholders, the capital budgeting process can be viewed as a search for investments with positive net present values.

 With our run-down house, you can probably imagine how we would go about making the capital budgeting decision. We would first look at what comparable, fixed-up properties were selling for in the market. We would then get estimates of the cost of buying a particular property and bringing it to market. At this point, we would have an estimated total cost and an estimated market value. If the difference was positive, then this investment would be worth undertaking because it would have a positive estimated net present value. There is risk, of course, because there is no guarantee that our estimates will turn out to be correct.

As our example illustrates, investment decisions are greatly simplified when there is a market for assets similar to the investment we are considering. An investment is worth undertaking if it creates value for its owners. In the most general sense, we create value by identifying an investment worth more in the marketplace than it costs us to acquire. How can something be worth more than it costs? It's a case of the whole being worth more than the cost of the parts.

For example, suppose you buy a run-down house for $25,000 and spend another $25,000 on painters, plumbers, and so on to get it fixed up. Your total investment is $50,000. When the work is completed, you place the house back on the market and find that it's worth $60,000. The market value ($60,000) exceeds the cost ($50,000) by $10,000. What you have done here is to act as a manager and bring together some fixed assets (a house), some labor (plumbers, carepners, and others), and some materials (carpeting, paint, and so on). The net result is that you have created $10,000 in value. Put another way, this $10,000 is the _value added_ by management.

With our house example, it turned out _after the fact_ that $10,000 in value had been created. Things thus worked out nicely. The real challenge, of course, would have been to somehow identify _ahead of time_ whether investing the necessary $50,000 was a good idea in the first place. This is what capital budgeting is all about--namely, trying to determine whether a proposed investment or project will be worth more, once it is in place, than it costs.

For reasons that will be obvious in a moment, the difference between an investment's market value and its cost is called the **net present value** of the investment, abbreviated **NPV**. In other words, net present value is a measure of how much value is created or added today by undertaking an investment. Given our goal of creating value for the stockholders, the capital budgeting process can be viewed as a search for investments with positive net present values.

We would first look at what comparable, fixed-up properties were selling for in the market. We would then get estimates of the cost of buying a particular property and bringing it to market. At this point, we would have an estimated total cost and an estimated market value. If the difference was positive, then this investment would be worth undertaking because it would have a positive estimated net present value. There is risk, of course, because there is no guarantee that our estimates will turn out to be correct.

data.content:
Finance term: known dividend yield,Black–Scholes–Merton model
Definition: A rule is established to extend valuation results for European options on non-dividend-paying stocks to those on stocks that pay a known dividend yield \( q \). Dividends lead to a decrease in stock prices on the ex-dividend date equivalent to the dividend payment. When a stock with an initial price \( S_{0} \) grows to \( S_{T} \) over time \( T \) while paying a dividend yield \( q \), the price grows less than it would otherwise, leading to two equivalent scenarios: 

1. Stock starts at \( S_{0} \) with dividend yield \( q \).
2. Stock starts at \( S_{0}e^{-qT} \) with no dividends.

From this equivalence, a simple rule emerges: when valuing a European option for a stock paying a dividend yield \( q \) over time \( T \), reduce the current stock price from \( S_{0} \) to \( S_{0}e^{-qT} \) and then value the option as if the stock pays no dividends.

### Lower Bounds for Option Prices

For a European call option price \( c \) on a stock with dividend yield \( q \), the lower bound is given by:

\[
c \geq \max(S_{0}e^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}, 0) \tag{17.1}
\]

For a European put option price \( p \):

\[
p \geq \max(Ke^{-rT} - S_{0}e^{-qT}, 0) \tag{17.2}
\]

### Put-Call Parity

By substituting \( S_{0} \) with \( S_{0}e^{-qT} \) in put-call parity, the relationship becomes:

\[
c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_{0}e^{-qT} \tag{17.3}
\]

### Pricing Formulas

Replacing \( S_{0} \) with \( S_{0}e^{-qT} \) in the Black-Scholes-Merton formulas for European options leads to:

\[
c = S_{0}e^{-qT}N(d_{1}) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_{2}) \tag{17.4}
\]

\[
p = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_{2}) - S_{0}e^{-qT}N(-d_{1}) \tag{17.5}
\]

Where \( d_{1} \) and \( d_{2} \) are defined as:

\[
d_{1} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K) + (r - q + \sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
\]

\[
d_{2} = \frac{\ln(S_{0}/K) + (r - q - \sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} = d_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{T}
\]

These results were initially derived by Merton. Under the assumption that the dividend yield \( q \) is known but not constant, the equations still hold with \( q \) representing the average annualized dividend yield during the option's life.

### Differential Equation and Risk-Neutral Valuation

The differential equation governing the option price with dividend yield \( q \) modifies to:

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + (r - q)S\frac{\partial f}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}S^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}} = rf \tag{17.6}
\]

In a risk-neutral world, the expected growth rate of the stock price becomes \( r - q \), and the stock price process is expressed as:

\[
dS = (r - q)S\,dt + \sigma S\,dz \tag{17.7}
\]

To value a derivative linked to the stock providing dividend yield \( q \), set the expected growth at \( r - q \) and discount at rate \( r \). The expected payoff for a call option in a risk-neutral environment is:

\[
e^{(r - q)T}S_{0}N(d_{1}) - KN(d_{2})
\]

Discounting gives rise to the option price formulation in equation (17.4).

question:
Despite its shortcomings, payback period is often used due to its simplicity and the ready availability of accounting numbers and estimates. It can be useful for short-term projects where liquidity is important.Which one of the following is an advantage of using the payback period to evaluate cash flows?

Options:
A. It accurately considers the time value of money.
B. It is the most comprehensive method for long-term project evaluation.
C. The analysis is straightforward and simple.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: undiscounted cash flow and,Discounted payback period
Definition: The **discounted payback period** addresses a key limitation of the traditional payback period rule, which does not consider the time value of money. It is defined as the time until the sum of discounted cash flows equals the initial investment. According to the **discounted payback rule**, an investment is deemed acceptable if its discounted payback is less than a specified number of years.

To compute the discounted payback period, consider a scenario with an initial investment of $300 requiring a 12.5 percent return, producing cash flows of $100 per year for five years. Each cash flow is discounted at 12.5 percent, and their totals are recorded in Table 3. The ordinary payback occurs after three years, but the discounted cash flows total $300 only after four years, indicating a discounted payback of four years.

Interpreting the discounted payback is crucial: the ordinary payback reflects accounting break-even, while the discounted payback encapsulates economic or financial break-even. In this case, it signifies that the initial investment, along with potential interest from alternative investments, is recovered within four years.

Figure 3 illustrates this concept by comparing the **future** value at 12.5 percent of the $300 investment to the **future** value of the annual cash flows. The intersection of these two values at four years indicates the cash flows exceed the original investment.

An essential characteristic of the discounted payback period is its implication on net present value (NPV). If a project has a discounted payback, it must have a positive NPV, as the NPV is zero when the sum of discounted cash flows equals the initial investment. For example, the present value of cash flows in Table 3 is $355 against an investment of $300, yielding a positive NPV of $55. This positive value represents cash flows occurring after the discounted payback. Consequently, adopting the discounted payback rule helps avoid projects with negative estimated NPVs.

Despite the advantages, the discounted payback period is seldom used in practice. The calculation is not significantly simpler than NPV, as it requires discounting cash flows and summing them, similar to the NPV approach. Furthermore, the analytical method has important limitations: a predetermined cutoff period must be arbitrarily established, and cash flows beyond this point are disregarded. This can lead to rejection of projects that might possess a positive NPV due to the inadequacy of the cutoff length. Additionally, a shorter discounted payback relative to another project does not imply a larger NPV.

Overall, the discounted payback period serves as a middle ground between the ordinary payback and NPV, offering a more refined approach that accounts for time value. It acknowledges the potential returns from alternative investments, an aspect overlooked by the traditional payback method.

\end{table}

An unanticipated decline in the price level can negatively affect lending practices.Which one of the following consequences can result from an unanticipated decline in the price level?

A. Increase in the real value of firms' assets
B. Increase in firms' real burden of indebtedness
C. Decrease in adverse selection and moral hazard
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Unanticipated Decline in the Price Level,Asset Market Effects on Balance Sheets,Factors Causing Financial Crisis
Definition: Unanticipated declines in the aggregate price level decrease the net worth of firms. Because debt payments are contractually fixed in nominal terms, an unanticipated decline in the price level raises the value of borrowing firms' liabilities in real terms (increases the burden of the debt) but does not raise the real value of firms' assets. The result is that net worth in real terms (the difference between assets and liabilities in real terms) declines. A sharp drop in the price level therefore causes a substantial decline in real net worth for borrowing firms and an increase in adverse selection and moral hazard problems facing lenders. An unanticipated decline in the aggregate price level thus leads to a drop in lending and economic activity.

In recent years, large financial institutions such as mutual funds and pension funds have been becoming dominant owners of stock in the United States, and these institutions are becoming more active in corporate affairs.Which one of the following is a potential implication of the increasing dominance of large financial institutions in the ownership of stock in the United States?

instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: control of the firm and,acting in the stockholders’ interests,Agency problem
Definition: Control of the firm ultimately rests with stockholders. They elect the board of directors, who in turn hire and fire managers. The fact that stockholders control the corporation was made abundantly clear by Steven Jobs's experience at Apple. Even though he was a founder of the corporation and was largely responsible for its most successful products, there came a time when shareholders, through their elected directors, decided that Apple would be better off without him, so out the went. Of course, he was later rehired and helped turn Apple around with great new products such as the iPod.

An important mechanism by which unhappy stockholders can act to replace existing management is called a _proxy fight_. A proxy is the authority to vote someone else's stock. A proxy fight develops when a group solicits proxies in order to replace the existing board and thereby replace existing managers. For example, in early 2002, the proposed merger between Hewlett-Packard (HP) and Compaq triggered one of the most widely followed, bitterly contested, and expensive proxy fights in history, with an estimated price tag of well over $100 million. One group of shareholders, which included Walter B. Hewlett (a board member and heir to a cofounder of HP), opposed the merger and launched a proxy fight for control of HP. Another group, led by HP CEO Carly Fiorina, supported the merger. In a very close vote, Ms. Fiorina prevailed, the merger went through, and Mr. Hewlett resigned from the board.

Another way that managers can be replaced is by takeover. Firms that are poorly managed are more attractive as acquisitions than well-managed firms because a greater profit potential exists. Thus, avoiding a takeover by another firm gives management another incentive to act in the stockholders' interests. For example, in April 2006, the management of Arcelo SA was attempting to fight off a bid from rival steelmaker Mittal Steel Co. Arcelo's management undertook several steps in an attempt to defeat the 20.4 billion ($24.8 billion) bid. First, the company transferred its lucrative Canadian operations to a Dutch foundation. Next, the company increased its dividend and promised a special dividend to shareholders when Mittal dropped its bid or the takeover failed. These payments to shareholders meant that remaining with current management or siding with Mittal would be financially equivalent.

options.B: Reduction in agency problems for U.S. corporations
options.C: Lower efficiency in the market for corporate control

data.content:
Finance term: rational expectations,The Theory of Rational Expectations
Definition: **Rational expectations** can be stated as follows: **Expectations will be identical to optimal forecasts** (_the best guess of the future_) **using all available information.
Formally, if X stands for the variable that is being forecast, X^{e} for the expectation of this variable, and X^{of} for the optimal forecast of X using all available information (the best guess possible of his driving time), the theory of rational expectations then simply says
X^{e}=X^{of}
That is, the expectation of X equals the optimal forecast using all available information.
Rational Behind the Theory: The incentives for equating expectations with optimal forecasts are especially strong in financial markets. In these markets, people with better forecasts of the future get rich. The application of the theory of rational expectations to financial markets (where it is called the **efficient market hypothesis** or the **theory of efficient capital markets**) is thus particularly useful.
Implications of the Theory are as follows:
1. _If there is a change in the way a variable moves, the way in which expectations of this variable are formed will change as well_.
2. _The forecast errors of expectations will, on average, be zero and cannot be predicted ahead of time_.

question:
Dollarization is a monetary system where a country adopts a foreign currency in place of its own.Which one of the following is a key advantage of dollarization?

Options:
A. Increases the revenue from seignorage
B. Eliminates the possibility of a speculative attack
C. Improves the country's ability to print its own money
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: Dollarization,To Peg or Not to Peg: Exchange-Rate Targeting as an Alternative Monetary Policy Strategy
Definition: Another solution to the problems created by a lack of transparency and commitment to the exchange-rate target is **dollarization**, the adoption of a sound currency, like the U.S. dollar, as a country's money. Indeed, dollarization is just another variant of a fixed exchange-rate target with an even stronger commitment mechanism than a currency board provides. A currency board can be abandoned, allowing a change in the value of the currency, but a change of value is impossible with dollarization: A dollar bill is always worth one dollar, whether it is held in the United States or outside of it. 
Dollarization has been advocated as a monetary policy strategy for emerging market countries: It was discussed actively by Argentine officials in the aftermath of the
devaluation of the Brazilian real in January 1999 and was adopted by Ecuador in March 2000. Dollarization's key advantage is that it completely avoids the possibility of a speculative attack on the domestic currency (because there is none). (Such an attack is still a danger even under a currency board arrangement.)
Dollarization is subject to the usual disadvantages of an exchange-rate target (the loss of an independent monetary policy, increased exposure of the economy to shocks from the anchor country, and the inability of the central bank to create money and act as a lender of last resort). Dollarization has one additional disadvantage not characteristic of currency boards or other exchange-rate target regimes. Because a country adopting dollarization no longer has its own currency, it loses the revenue that a government receives by issuing money, which is called **seignorage**. Because governments (or their central banks) do not have to pay interest on their currency, they earn revenue (seignorage) by using this currency to purchase income-earning assets such as bonds. In the case of the Federal Reserve in the United States, this revenue is on the order of $30 billion per year. If an emerging market country dollarizes and gives up its currency, it needs to make up this loss of revenue somewhere, which is not always easy for a poor country.

options.B: Eliminates the possibility of a speculative attack
options.C: Improves the country's ability to print its own money

C. The buyer of protection sells bonds issued by the reference entity for their face value.
instruction: Solve the financial reasoning problem using the provided information. Return only the final answer.

data.content:
Finance term: credit default swaps,Duration
Definition: The precise way in which CDS and CDS index transactions work is a little more complicated than has been described up to now. For each underlying and each maturity, a coupon and a recovery rate are specified. A price is calculated from the quoted spread using the following procedure:

1. Assume four payments per year, made in arrears.
2. Imply a hazard rate from the quoted spread. This involves calculations similar to those in Section 25.2. An iterative search is used to determine the hazard rate that leads to the quoted spread.
3. Calculate a "duration" \(D\) for the CDS payments. This is the number that the spread is multiplied by to get the present value of the spread payments. (In the example in Section 25.2, it is 4.1130.)7 Footnote 7: This use of the term “duration” is different from that in Chapter 4.
4. The price \(P\) is given by \(P=100-100\times D\times(s-c)\), where \(s\) is the spread and \(c\) is the coupon expressed in decimal form.

When a trader buys protection the trader pays \(100-P\) per $100 of the total remaining notional and the seller of protection receives this amount. (If \(100-P\) is negative, the buyer of protection receives money and the seller of protection pays money.) The buyer of protection then pays the coupon times the remaining notional on each payment date. (On a CDS, the remaining notional is the original notional until default and zero thereafter. For a CDS index, the remaining notional is the number of names in the index that have not yet defaulted multiplied by the principal per name.) The payoff when there is a default is calculated in the usual way. This arrangement facilitates trading because the instruments trade like bonds. The regular quarterly payments made by the buyer of protection are independent of the spread at the time the buyer enters into the contract.
